list of sessions\n        [  # list of trials for session 1\n            neuron_by_time_matrix,  # shape: (n_neurons, n_timepoints)\n            neuron_by_time_matrix,  # trial 2\n            ...\n        ],\n        [  # They could be task inputs to the animal, but inputs to the animal can also be decoder outputs.\n  - Examples: time from an aligning signal, stimulus characteristics, our animal behavior such as:\n    - visual: contrast, position, orientation\n    - audio: frequency, amplitude\n    - behavior: running speed, pupil size\n  - Dimensions: (d_input, n_timepoints) for each trial. \n  - Should capture all relevant contextual information for the decoder\n  - If an input is a time such as onset of some stimulus, represent it as a binary time series. \n\n- **output**: Variables to be decoded/predicted from neural activity\n  - These are what we want the decoder to **predict**. They could be the animal's output behavior or properties of the stimulus.\n  - Output variables must be **categorical**, i.e. discrete rather than continuous. If at all possible, make it time-varying\n  - If an output is a time such as when a behavior occurred, represent it as a binary time series. \n\n- **subjects**: List of names of all unique subjects (mice).\n- **subject_idx**: Index into subjects for each session.\n  - Order should match order of sessions in `neural`, etc.\n\n- **brain_regions**: List of names of all brain regions recorded from.\n- **brain_region_idx**: Index into brain_regions for each neuron in each session.\n\n- **input_names**: Names of each input variable.\n  - Order should match order of `input` dimensions. \n\n- **output_names**: Names of each output variable.\n  - Order should match order of `output` dimensions.\n- **output_values**: Names of each output value for each output variable.\n  - Order should match categorical `output` values.\n\n- **metadata**: Descriptive information. \n  - `task_description`: Concise description of the task\n  - `temporal_alignment_event`: Concise description of temporal alignment event\n  - `off_start`: Signed time from alignment event to start of trial. list of sessions\n        [  # list of trials for session 1\n            neuron_by_time_matrix,  # shape: (n_neurons, n_timepoints)\n            neuron_by_time_matrix,  # trial 2\n            ...\n        ],\n        [  # list of trials for session 2\n            ...\n        ],\n        ...\n    ],\n\n    'input': [  # list of sessions\n        [  # list of trials for session 1\n            input_data,  # stimulus/task variables, shape: (n_input, n_timepoints) or (n_input)\n            ...\n        ],\n        ...\n    ],\n\n    'output': [  # list of sessions\n        [  # list of trials for session 1\n            output_data,  # behavioral response, shape (n_output, n_timepoints) or (n_output)\n            ...\n        ],\n        ...\n    ],\n\n    'subjects': list of str, # ids of all subjects, length n_subjects\n    'subject_idx': shape (n_sessions,), # index into subjects for each session\n\n    'brain_regions': list of str, # names of the brain regions recorded from, e.g. ALM, V1\n    'brain_region_idx': [ # list of sessions\n        neuron_region_idx, # shape: (n_neurons,)\n    ], # index into `brain_regions` for each neuron\n\n    'input_names': list of str, # names for each input, of length n_input\n    'output_names': list of str, # names of each output, of length n_output\n    'output_values': [ # list of length n_output\n        [ output_val0, ... ], # list of str of length d_output[0], name of each output value\n        ...\n    ],\n\n    'metadata': {\n        'task_description': str, # description of output tasks\n        'time_bin_size': float, # length of time bin in ms\n        'temporal_alignment_event': str, # description of alignment event\n        'off_start': float or None, # signed time from alignment event to start of trial in seconds, None if N/A\n        'off_end': float or None, # signed time from alignment event to end of trial in seconds, None if N/A\n        ...\n    }\n}\n```\n\n### Key Format Requirements\n\n- **neural**: Neural activity data (e.g., firing rates, spike counts) organized by session and trial\n  - Dimensions: (n_neurons, n_timepoints) for each trial.\n  - Time bins should be the same size for all trials and sessions. \n  - There needs to be at least two trials within each session in order to evaluate the decoder performance.\n\n- **input**: Variables that serve as inputs **to the decoder**\n  - These are **decoder inputs**. They could be task inputs to the animal, but inputs to the animal can also be decoder outputs.\n  - Examples: time from an aligning signal, stimulus characteristics, our animal behavior such as:\n    - visual: contrast, position, orientation\n    - audio: frequency, amplitude\n    - behavior: running speed, pupil size\n  - Dimensions: (d_input, n_timepoints) for each trial. \n  - Should capture all relevant contextual information for the decoder\n  - If an input is a time such as onset of some stimulus, represent it as a binary time series. \n\n- **output**: Variables to be decoded/predicted from neural activity\n  - These are what we want the decoder to **predict**. They could be the animal's output behavior or properties of the stimulus.\n  - Output variables must be **categorical**, i.e. discrete rather than continuous. If a variable is not discrete, follow instructions from Decoder Task to discretize it. \n  - Examples: stimulus properties (contrast, orientation), choice (left/right), reaction time, position\n  - Can be time-varying or discrete values per trial. If at all possible, make it time-varying\n  - If an output is a time such as when a behavior occurred, represent it as a binary time series. \n\n- **subjects**: List of names of all unique subjects (mice).\n- **subject_idx**: Index into subjects for each session.\n  - Order should match order of sessions in `neural`, etc.\n\n- **brain_regions**: List of names of all brain regions recorded from.\n- **brain_region_idx**: Index into brain_regions for each neuron in each session.\n\n- **input_names**: Names of each input variable.\n  - Order should match order of `input` dimensions. \n\n- **output_names**: Names of each output variable.\n  - Order should match order of `output` dimensions.\n- **output_values**: Names of each output value for each output variable.\n  - Order should match categorical `output` values.\n\n- **metadata**: Descriptive information. \n  - `task_description`: Concise description of the task\n  - `temporal_alignment_event`: Concise description of temporal alignment event\n  - `off_start`: Signed time from alignment event to start of trial. Negative means before event, positive after. \n  - `off_end`: Signed time from alignment event to end of trial\n  - Add other relevant fields, e.g. `session_info`\n\n## Python environment\n\n- All required Python packages are already installed in the system Python environment.\n- Use `python3` to run any python code.\n- If you need to install additional libraries, use `pip install`.\n\n## Decoder Reference\n\n- Run this script with `python /app/train_decoder.py <data_file_path>` to validate.\n- Optional arguments:\n  - `--verify-only`: Only verify data format and print summary, then exit (does not train decoder).\n  - `--plot-samples`: Plot sample trials from data and save to png files.\n  - `--cpu`: Force torch to use CPU only (use if GPU runs out of memory).\n- Pipe the output to the designated file so that the user can examine it.\n\n### Purpose\n\nThese functions will be used during the validation phase to ensure:\n1. Data structure is correct - will report errors and warnings to stdout. \n2. Dimensions are consistent - will report errors and warnings to stdout. \n3. Values are sensible - will report errors and warnings to stdout. \n4. Decoder can successfully train and predict\n5. Poor performance indicates data formatting issues that need investigation\n\n### Consistency requirements\n\nYour processing and formatting must **match the reference papers and code** with respect to:\n- Loading of data\n- Temporal alignment of different time series streams (neural, inputs, outputs)\n- Processing of neural, input, and output data streams\n- Curation of data: filtering of low-quality neurons, trials, sessions, and mice.\n\nTo check consistency, you must compare statistics available in the reference paper and your converted dataset. \n\nWhenever possible, invent **SANITY CHECKS** that your loading and processing matches the reference paper and code. \n\nDiscrepancies are only allowed if required by the Decoder Input and Decoder Output specifications above, or the task of training a neural decoder.\n\nCarefully verify your work after every step. It is in the file `/app/methodpaper.pdf`\n30\t  - A white paper about spike sorting and quality control is in the file `/app/ChenLiuEtAl2023_SpikeSortingQC.pdf`\n31\t- Some parts of the paper that describe the experiment and processing have been copied to the file `/app/methods.txt`. \n32\t- **Code**:\n33\t  - `/app/code` contains code from `/app/methodpaper.pdf`.\n34\t- **Data** from the papers are in the directory `/app/data`.\n35\t- **Documentation** on the **NWB** file format is at https://nwb-schema.readthedocs.io. Documentation about `pynwb` is at https://pynwb.readthedocs.io/en/stable/. `pynwb` documentation is also downloaded to `/app/pynwb_docs/`.\n36\t\n37\t## Decoder Task\n38\t\n39\t- Temporally align based on **Go cue onset**. \n40\t- Extract **2.5 s before to 1.5 s after** the go cue for each trial\n41\t- Use **50-ms-width bins** for computing firing rates. \n42\t\n43\t### Decoder Inputs:\n44\t- Time from **tone onset** in seconds (continuous, time-varying)\n45\t- Whether **photostimulation** is on at every time point (discrete, time-varying)\n46\t\n47\t### Decoder Outputs\n48\t- Lick direction **choice** (left, right, no lick, per-trial)\n49\t- **Outcome** (ignore, miss, hit, per-trial)\n50\t- **Early lick** (no, yes, per-trial)\n51\t- **Tongue y-position**, per-session discretization:\n52\t  - 0: < 40th percentile of y-position over the session\n53\t  - 1: 40th to 60th percentile of y-position over the session\n54\t  - 2: > 60th percentile of y-position over the session\n55\t  - 3: not visible\n56\t\n57\t## Target Data Format\n58\t\n59\t- Save the full converted dataset to the pickle file `/app/converted_data.pkl`.\n60\t- All datasets must be converted into the following Python dictionary structure:\n61\t\n62\t```python\n63\tdata = {\n64\t    'neural': [  # list of sessions\n65\t        [  # list of trials for session 1\n66\t            neuron_by_time_matrix,  # shape: (n_neurons, n_timepoints)\n67\t            neuron_by_time_matrix,  # trial 2\n68\t            ...\n69\t        ],\n70\t        [  # list of trials for session 2\n71\t            ...\n72\t        ],\n73\t        ...\n74\t    ],\n75\t\n76\t    'input': [  # list of sessions\n77\t        [  # list of trials for session 1\n78\t            input_data,  # stimulus/task variables, shape: (n_input, n_timepoints) or (n_input)\n79\t            ...\n80\t        ],\n81\t        ...\n82\t    ],\n83\t\n84\t    'output': [  # list of sessions\n85\t        [  # list of trials for session 1\n86\t            output_data,  # behavioral response, shape (n_output, n_timepoints) or (n_output)\n87\t            ...\n88\t        ],\n89\t        ...\n90\t    ],\n91\t\n92\t    'subjects': list of str, # ids of all subjects, length n_subjects\n93\t    'subject_idx': shape (n_sessions,), # index into subjects for each session\n94\t\n95\t    'brain_regions': list of str, # names of the brain regions recorded from, e.g. ALM, V1\n96\t    'brain_region_idx': [ # list of sessions\n97\t        neuron_region_idx, # shape: (n_neurons,)\n98\t    ], # index into `brain_regions` for each neuron\n99\t\n100\t    'input_names': list of str, # names for each input, of length n_input\n101\t    'output_names': list of str, # names of each output, of length n_output\n102\t    'output_values': [ # list of length n_output\n103\t        [ output_val0, ... ], # list of str of length d_output[0], name of each output value\n104\t        ...\n105\t    ],\n106\t\n107\t    'metadata': {\n108\t        'task_description': str, # description of output tasks\n109\t        'time_bin_size': float, # length of time bin in ms\n110\t        'temporal_alignment_event': str, # description of alignment event\n111\t        'off_start': float or None, # signed time from alignment event to start of trial in seconds, None if N/A\n112\t        'off_end': float or None, # signed time from alignment event to end of trial in seconds, None if N/A\n113\t        ...\n114\t    }\n115\t}\n116\t```\n117\t\n118\t### Key Format Requirements\n119\t\n120\t- **neural**: Neural activity data (e.g., firing rates, spike counts) organized by session and trial\n121\t  - Dimensions: (n_neurons, n_timepoints) for each trial.\n122\t  - Time bins should be the same size for all trials and sessions. \n123\t  - There needs to be at least two trials within each session in order to evaluate the decoder performance.\n124\t\n125\t- **input**: Variables that serve as inputs **to the decoder**\n126\t  - These are **decoder inputs**. They could be task inputs to the animal, but inputs to the animal can also be decoder outputs.\n127\t  - Examples: time from an aligning signal, stimulus characteristics, our animal behavior such as:\n128\t    - visual: contrast, position, orientation\n129\t    - audio: frequency, amplitude\n130\t    - behavior: running speed, pupil size\n131\t  - Dimensions: (d_input, n_timepoints) for each trial. \n132\t  - Should capture all relevant contextual information for the decoder\n133\t  - If an input is a time such as onset of some stimulus, represent it as a binary time series. \n134\t\n135\t- **output**: Variables to be decoded/predicted from neural activity\n136\t  - These are what we want the decoder to **predict**. They could be the animal's output behavior or properties of the stimulus.\n137\t  - Output variables must be **categorical**, i.e. discrete rather than continuous. If a variable is not discrete, follow instructions from Decoder Task to discretize it. \n138\t  - Examples: stimulus properties (contrast, orientation), choice (left/right), reaction time, position\n139\t  - Can be time-varying or discrete values per trial. If at all possible, make it time-varying\n140\t  - If an output is a time such as when a behavior occurred, represent it as a binary time series. \n141\t\n142\t- **subjects**: List of names of all unique subjects (mice).\n143\t- **subject_idx**: Index into subjects for each session.\n144\t  - Order should match order of sessions in `neural`, etc.\n145\t\n146\t- **brain_regions**: List of names of all brain regions recorded from.\n147\t- **brain_region_idx**: Index into brain_regions for each neuron in each session.\n148\t\n149\t- **input_names**: Names of each input variable.\n150\t  - Order should match order of `input` dimensions. \n151\t\n152\t- **output_names**: Names of each output variable.\n153\t  - Order should match order of `output` dimensions.\n154\t- **output_values**: Names of each output value for each output variable.\n155\t  - Order should match categorical `output` values.\n156\t\n157\t- **metadata**: Descriptive information. \n158\t  - `task_description`: Concise description of the task\n159\t  - `temporal_alignment_event`: Concise description of temporal alignment event\n160\t  - `off_start`: Signed time from alignment event to start of trial. Negative means before event, positive after. \n161\t  - `off_end`: Signed time from alignment event to end of trial\n162\t  - Add other relevant fields, e.g. `session_info`\n163\t\n164\t## Python environment\n165\t\n166\t- All required Python packages are already installed in the system Python environment.\n167\t- Use `python3` to run any python code.\n168\t- If you need to install additional libraries, use `pip install`.\n169\t\n170\t## Decoder Reference\n171\t\n172\t- Run this script with `python /app/train_decoder.py <data_file_path>` to validate.\n173\t- Optional arguments:\n174\t  - `--verify-only`: Only verify data format and print summary, then exit (does not train decoder).\n175\t  - `--plot-samples`: Plot sample trials from data and save to png files.\n176\t  - `--cpu`: Force torch to use CPU only (use if GPU runs out of memory).\n177\t- Pipe the output to the designated file so that the user can examine it.\n178\t\n179\t### Purpose\n180\t\n181\tThese functions will be used during the validation phase to ensure:\n182\t1. Documentation about `pynwb` is at https://pynwb.readthedocs.io/en/stable/. `pynwb` documentation is also downloaded to `/app/pynwb_docs/`.\n\n## Decoder Task\n\n- Temporally align based on **Go cue onset**. \n- Extract **2.5 s before to 1.5 s after** the go cue for each trial\n- Use **50-ms-width bins** for computing firing rates. \n\n### Decoder Inputs:\n- Time from **tone onset** in seconds (continuous, time-varying)\n- Whether **photostimulation** is on at every time point (discrete, time-varying)\n\n### Decoder Outputs\n- Lick direction **choice** (left, right, no lick, per-trial)\n- **Outcome** (ignore, miss, hit, per-trial)\n- **Early lick** (no, yes, per-trial)\n- **Tongue y-position**, per-session discretization:\n  - 0: < 40th percentile of y-position over the session\n  - 1: 40th to 60th percentile of y-position over the session\n  - 2: > 60th percentile of y-position over the session\n  - 3: not visible\n\n## Target Data Format\n\n- Save the full converted dataset to the pickle file `/app/converted_data.pkl`.\n- All datasets must be converted into the following Python dictionary structure:\n\n```python\ndata = {\n    'neural': [  # list of sessions\n        [  # list of trials for session 1\n            neuron_by_time_matrix,  # shape: (n_neurons, n_timepoints)\n            neuron_by_time_matrix,  # trial 2\n            ...\n        ],\n        [  # list of trials for session 2\n            ...\n        ],\n        ...\n    ],\n\n    'input': [  # list of sessions\n        [  # list of trials for session 1\n            input_data,  # stimulus/task variables, shape: (n_input, n_timepoints) or (n_input)\n            ...\n        ],\n        ...\n    ],\n\n    'output': [  # list of sessions\n        [  # list of trials for session 1\n            output_data,  # behavioral response, shape (n_output, n_timepoints) or (n_output)\n            ...\n        ],\n        ...\n    ],\n\n    'subjects': list of str, # ids of all subjects, length n_subjects\n    'subject_idx': shape (n_sessions,), # index into subjects for each session\n\n    'brain_regions': list of str, # names of the brain regions recorded from, e.g. ALM, V1\n    'brain_region_idx': [ # list of sessions\n        neuron_region_idx, # shape: (n_neurons,)\n    ], # index into `brain_regions` for each neuron\n\n    'input_names': list of str, # names for each input, of length n_input\n    'output_names': list of str, # names of each output, of length n_output\n    'output_values': [ # list of length n_output\n        [ output_val0, ... ], # list of str of length d_output[0], name of each output value\n        ...\n    ],\n\n    'metadata': {\n        'task_description': str, # description of output tasks\n        'time_bin_size': float, # length of time bin in ms\n        'temporal_alignment_event': str, # description of alignment event\n        'off_start': float or None, # signed time from alignment event to start of trial in seconds, None if N/A\n        'off_end': float or None, # signed time from alignment event to end of trial in seconds, None if N/A\n        ...\n    }\n}\n```\n\n### Key Format Requirements\n\n- **neural**: Neural activity data (e.g., firing rates, spike counts) organized by session and trial\n  - Dimensions: (n_neurons, n_timepoints) for each trial.\n  - Time bins should be the same size for all trials and sessions. \n  - There needs to be at least two trials within each session in order to evaluate the decoder performance.\n\n- **input**: Variables that serve as inputs **to the decoder**\n  - These are **decoder inputs**. They could be task inputs to the animal, but inputs to the animal can also be decoder outputs.\n  - Examples: time from an aligning signal, stimulus characteristics, our animal behavior such as:\n    - visual: contrast, position, orientation\n    - audio: frequency, amplitude\n    - behavior: running speed, pupil size\n  - Dimensions: (d_input, n_timepoints) for each trial. \n  - Should capture all relevant contextual information for the decoder\n  - If an input is a time such as onset of some stimulus, represent it as a binary time series. \n\n- **output**: Variables to be decoded/predicted from neural activity\n  - These are what we want the decoder to **predict**. They could be the animal's output behavior or properties of the stimulus.\n  - Output variables must be **categorical**, i.e. discrete rather than continuous. If a variable is not discrete, follow instructions from Decoder Task to discretize it. \n  - Examples: stimulus properties (contrast, orientation), choice (left/right), reaction time, position\n  - Can be time-varying or discrete values per trial. If at all possible, make it time-varying\n  - If an output is a time such as when a behavior occurred, represent it as a binary time series. \n\n- **subjects**: List of names of all unique subjects (mice).\n- **subject_idx**: Index into subjects for each session.\n  - Order should match order of sessions in `neural`, etc.\n\n- **brain_regions**: List of names of all brain regions recorded from.\n- **brain_region_idx**: Index into brain_regions for each neuron in each session.\n\n- **input_names**: Names of each input variable.\n  - Order should match order of `input` dimensions. \n\n- **output_names**: Names of each output variable.\n  - Order should match order of `output` dimensions.\n- **output_values**: Names of each output value for each output variable.\n  - Order should match categorical `output` values.\n\n- **metadata**: Descriptive information. \n  - `task_description`: Concise description of the task\n  - `temporal_alignment_event`: Concise description of temporal alignment event\n  - `off_start`: Signed time from alignment event to start of trial. Negative means before event, positive after. \n  - `off_end`: Signed time from alignment event to end of trial\n  - Add other relevant fields, e.g. `session_info`\n\n## Python environment\n\n- All required Python packages are already installed in the system Python environment.\n- Use `python3` to run any python code.\n- If you need to install additional libraries, use `pip install`.\n\n## Decoder Reference\n\n- Run this script with `python /app/train_decoder.py <data_file_path>` to validate.\n- Optional arguments:\n  - `--verify-only`: Only verify data format and print summary, then exit (does not train decoder).\n  - `--plot-samples`: Plot sample trials from data and save to png files.\n  - `--cpu`: Force torch to use CPU only (use if GPU runs out of memory).\n- Pipe the output to the designated file so that the user can examine it.\n\n### Purpose\n\nThese functions will be used during the validation phase to ensure:\n1. Data structure is correct - will report errors and warnings to stdout. \n2. Dimensions are consistent - will report errors and warnings to stdout. \n3. Values are sensible - will report errors and warnings to stdout. \n4. Decoder can successfully train and predict\n5. Poor performance indicates data formatting issues that need investigation\n\n### Consistency requirements\n\nYour processing and formatting must **match the reference papers and code** with respect to:\n- Loading of data\n- Temporal alignment of different time series streams (neural, inputs, outputs)\n- Processing of neural, input, and output data streams\n- Curation of data: filtering of low-quality neurons, trials, sessions, and mice.\n\nTo check consistency, you must compare statistics available in the reference paper and your converted dataset. \n\nWhenever possible, invent **SANITY CHECKS** that your loading and processing matches the reference paper and code. \n\nDiscrepancies are only allowed if required by the Decoder Input and Decoder Output specifications above, or the task of training a neural decoder.\n\nCarefully verify your work after every step. When you find mistakes, document and fix them immediately. a large jump invalidates the frame after the jump\n218\t            valid[iv[1:][bad]] = False\n219\t    res = np.full((ntr, NBINS), np.nan, dtype=np.float32)\n220\t    t0 = go_times + OFF_START\n221\t    lo = np.searchsorted(ts, t0)\n222\t    hi = np.searchsorted(ts, go_times + OFF_END)\n223\t    for i in range(ntr):\n224\t        a, b = lo[i], hi[i]\n225\t        if b <= a:\n226\t            continue\n227\t        tsel = ts[a:b]\n228\t        vsel = valid[a:b]\n229\t        if not vsel.any():\n230\t            continue\n231\t        bi = np.floor((tsel[vsel] - t0[i]) / BIN_SIZE).astype(int)\n232\t        np.clip(bi, 0, NBINS - 1, out=bi)\n233\t        cnt = np.bincount(bi, minlength=NBINS)\n234\t        sm = np.bincount(bi, weights=y[a:b][vsel], minlength=NBINS)\n235\t        nz = cnt > 0\n236\t        res[i, nz] = (sm[nz] / cnt[nz]).astype(np.float32)\n237\t    return res\n238\t\n239\t\n240\tdef discretize_tongue(y_binned):\n241\t    \"\"\"Per-session discretisation of tongue y into 4 classes (task specification).\"\"\"\n242\t    vis = np.isfinite(y_binned)\n243\t    cls = np.full(y_binned.shape, 3, dtype=np.int64)     # 3 = not visible\n244\t    if vis.sum() > 0:\n245\t        p40, p60 = np.percentile(y_binned[vis], [40, 60])\n246\t        v = y_binned[vis]\n247\t        c = np.where(v < p40, 0, np.where(v <= p60, 1, 2))\n248\t        cls[vis] = c\n249\t    else:\n250\t        p40 = p60 = np.nan\n251\t    return cls, float(p40), float(p60)\n252\t\n253\t\n254\t# ------------------------------------------------------------------- per-session conversion\n255\tdef convert_session(path, show_processing=False):\n256\t    \"\"\"Convert one NWB session file; returns a dict or None if the session is dropped.\"\"\"\n257\t    t_start = time.time()\n258\t    timing = {}\n259\t    with NWBHDF5IO(path, mode='r', load_namespaces=True) as io:\n260\t        nwb = io.read()\n261\t        ident = nwb.identifier\n262\t        subject = str(nwb.subject.subject_id)\n263\t        subject_name = str(nwb.subject.description)\n264\t\n265\t        # reference midline convention\n283\t        groups = np.array([map_annotation(a) for a in anno])\n284\t        region_labels = np.array(['%s %s' % (s, g) for s, g in zip(side, groups)])\n285\t        timing['units_meta'] = time.time() - t0\n286\t\n287\t        #                                 np.where(instr_k == 'left', 1, 0))).astype(np.int64)\n359\t        outcome_code = np.where(out_k == 'ignore', 0, np.where(out_k == 'miss', 1, tone_onset_times(sample_starts, trial_starts, go_times):\n    \"\"\"Last sample(tone)-epoch start at or before the go cue, for each trial.\n\n    Early licking triggers a replay of the sample/delay epoch, so a trial can contain several\n    `sample_start_times`; the *last* one before the go cue is the tone the animal responded to.\n    \"\"\"\n    ntr = len(go_times)\n    out = np.full(ntr, out[tidx[order]] = ev[order]\n    return out\n\n\ndef photostim_binary(stim_on, stim_off, trial_starts, go_times):\n    \"\"\"(n_trials, NBINS) binary array: is photostimulation on during this Following the method paper, frames with a 5-sigma velocity\n    outlier are discarded; unlike the method paper (which imputes the mean for occluded frames)\n    the decoder task asks for an explicit 'not visible' class, so bins without a valid visible\n    frame are left as NaN and encoded as class 3 downstream.\n    \"\"\"\n    ntr = len(go_times)\n    visible = lik > TONGUE_LIK_THRESH\n    valid = visible.copy()\n    if visible.sum() > 10:\n        iv = np.where(visible)[0]\n        dy = np.diff(y[iv]) / np.maximum(np.diff(ts[iv]), 1e-6)\n        s = np.std(dy)\n        if s > 0:\n            bad = np.abs(dy) > VELOCITY_SIGMA * s\n            # for our task we are instructed to use 50-ms bins, so we will use non-overlapping 50-ms bins (stride = width = 50 ms), which is the natural analogue.\n47\t- Epochs used in the paper (relative to go cue): sample `[-1.85, -1.2]` s, delay `[-1.2, 0]` s, response `[0, 1.5]` s. Our decoder task explicitly requires photostim as an input and early lick, no-lick choice and ignore/miss outcome as outputs, so those trials must be **kept**; we will only exclude auto-water/free-water trials (not real behaviour) if warranted, documented in Step 5.\n52\t\n53\t---\n54\t\n55\t## Step 2: Dataset Exploration\n56\t**Status**: COMPLETE\n57\t\n58\t### Data Structure\n59\t- `/app/data/` contains one directory per mouse: `sub-<subject_id>/` (28 subjects) and `dandiset.yaml` (DANDI:000363, Mesoscale Activity Map dataset, Chen et al.).\n60\t- Each session is one NWB file: `sub-<id>_ses-<YYYYMMDDTHHMMSS>_behavior+ecephys+ogen.nwb`; reference epochs sample [−1.85, −1.2] s, delay [−1.2, 0] s, response [0, 1.5] s.\n128\t- **Binning**: sliding 40 ms window, 3.4 ms stride, rates in Hz (spikes/bin_width). Our task specifies **50 ms bins**, which we implement as non-overlapping 50 ms bins giving rates in Hz (80 bins over −2.5→+1.5 s).\n129\t- **Spike sorting / QC**: Kilosort2 output; 15 quality metrics; five region-specific logistic-regression classifiers (cortex, striatum, thalamus, midbrain, medulla) trained on manual Phy labels; units labelled **`good`** are used for all analyses. In the NWB files this classifier output is the `units.classification` column (`good` vs `unlabelled`), and `anno_name` holds the CCF annotation of classified units. The whitepaper explicitly argues that thresholding individual metrics is inadequate — hence using the provided classifier label is the faithful reproduction of their QC.\n130\t- **Video markers**: DeepLabCut side-view tongue/jaw/nose; outliers detected by 5-sigma velocity threshold and imputed from nearby frames; when the tongue is occluded (in the mouth) the method paper sets tongue position to its mean value. Our decoder task instead requires an explicit \"not visible\" class (class 3), so occlusion is represented as its own category (detected via DLC likelihood).\n131\t- **Region grouping** (reference preprocessing loop): ALM, Medulla, Midbrain, Striatum, Thalamus, Pons, Cerebellum, Hypothalamus, Hippocampus, Orbital, OtherCortex, Olfactory, CorticalSubplate, Pallidum — each split into left/right hemisphere with the CCF ML midline at 5,700 µm.\n132\t\n133\t### Curation Steps\n134\t**Neuron curation rules (reference)**\n135\t1. Keep only units with a CCF/histology annotation (units without histology are dropped).\n136\t2. Keep only units labelled `good` by the QC classifier (25.9 % of Kilosort clusters).\n137\t3. Method-paper analyses additionally drop neurons with mean firing rate < 2 Hz (for firing-rate *prediction* analyses) and brain areas with < 10 neurons per session. These are analysis-specific and are **not** appropriate for the decoding task here (they would discard most of the population available to the decoder), so they are not applied; documented in Step 5.\n138\t\n139\t**Trial curation rules (reference)**\n140\t- \"regular\" trials = no early lick, no auto-water, no free water, no ignore (`correctness != -1`), and no photostimulation.\n141\t- **Our decoder task requires early-lick, photostim, ignore and miss trials** (they are explicit decoder inputs/outputs), so these filters are relaxed; see Step 5.\n142\t- Session inclusion criteria in the data paper (performance > 65 %, ≥ 50 correct left and right trials) are already satisfied by the published sessions.\n143\t\n144\t### Decoders Trained (reference accuracies)\n145\t| Decoded variable | Accuracy |\n146\t|---|---|\n147\t| Choice from behavioral video, pre-sample epoch | AUC 0.51 ± 0.06 (n = 106 sessions) |\n148\t| Choice from behavioral video, sample+delay epochs | AUC 0.66 ± 0.12 |\n149\t| Choice from behavioral video, second half of response epoch | AUC 0.99 ± 0.01 |\n150\t| Choice from single-neuron delay activity (AUC threshold for \"choice-modulated\") | AUC > 0.65 |\n151\t| Uninstructed-movement type from single neurons | AUC > 0.65 threshold |\n152\t\n153\tImplication for our decoder: **choice** should be decodable near-perfectly after the go cue from population activity (video alone gives AUC 0.99); delay-epoch choice information is weaker. Outcome and early-lick should be decodable well above chance; tongue position (a directly observable movement) should be decodable well, since neural activity predicts video markers with high R² in the method paper.\n154\t\n155\t---\n156\t\n157\t## Step 4: Check for Consistency\n158\t**Status**: COMPLETE\n159\t\n160\tI cross-checked the reference code (Step 1), the NWB data (Step 2) and the papers (Step 3). Auto-water and free-water trials (reward independent of the animal's action, 4 % of trials) are **excluded**, matching the reference, since their `outcome` label is not behaviourally meaningful. |\n175\t| Choice definition | `trial_type` (instruction) + `correctness` | `outcome` + `trial_instruction` reproduces the lick-derived choice in >99 % of trials (disagreements are `ignore` trials with a lick after the response window) | hit = licked instructed side, miss = licked other side, ignore = no lick | Choice := instructed side for `hit`, opposite side for `miss`, `no lick` for `ignore`. |\n176\t| Binning | 40 ms window / 3.4 ms stride (sliding) | spike times available at full resolution | same | Task specifies **50 ms bins** → non-overlapping 50 ms bins, rates in Hz (counts/0.05 s), 80 bins for −2.5→+1.5 s. |\n177\t| Observation window | spike times truncated to [−3, 3] s re go cue | `obs_intervals` == trial (start_time, stop_time); **all** spikes lie inside trials; 96.9 % of trials cover go−2.5 s and 84.4 % cover go+1.5 s (miss trials terminate ~0.8 s after the go cue) | n/a | Bins outside the trial's observed interval contain no spikes by construction; they are set to 0 and flagged in metadata. Dropping short trials is not an option (it would delete 95 % of `miss` trials and destroy the outcome output). |\n178\t\n179\t---\n180\t\n181\t## Step 5: Mapping Planning\n182\t**Status**: COMPLETE\n183\t\n184\t### Variable Mapping\n185\t| Source (NWB) | Target field | Transform | Reference-code counterpart | Notes |\n186\t|---|---|---|---|---|\n187\t| `units.spike_times` (session clock) for units with `classification == 'good'` | `neural[session][trial]` (n_neurons, 80) | subtract that trial's go-cue time; Unlabelled units also lack CCF annotations, so this simultaneously enforces the reference's \"must have histology\" rule. Result: 69,453 units (25.5 % of clusters) vs 69,943 (25.9 %) in the paper.\n200\t2. **No additional firing-rate threshold**: the method paper's ≥ 2 Hz filter and its \"≥10 neurons per area per session\" rule apply to their neuron-wise *encoding* analyses; for population decoding, discarding low-rate neurons throws away usable signal and is not part of the dataset-level curation. Not applied (documented deviation).\n201\t3. **Session curation**: drop sessions with 0 good units → exactly **173** sessions, matching the papers.\n202\t4. **Trial curation**: drop `auto_water == 1` or `free_water == 1` trials (reward delivered independent of the animal's action ⇒ `outcome` is not a behavioural report), matching `get_regular_trial_mask`. **Keep** early-lick, ignore/miss and photostim trials, because the decoder task defines them as outputs/inputs; the reference excluded them only for its encoding analyses.\n203\t5. **Alignment / window / binning**: go-cue aligned, −2.5 → +1.5 s, 80 × 50 ms non-overlapping bins, rates in Hz (counts / 0.05 s). reference epochs sample [−1.85, −1.2] s, delay [−1.2, 0] s, response [0, 1.5] s.\n- **Binning**: sliding 40 ms window, 3.4 ms stride, rates in Hz (spikes/bin_width). Our task specifies **50 ms bins**, which we implement as non-overlapping 50 ms bins giving rates in Hz (80 bins over −2.5→+1.5 s).\n- **Spike sorting / QC**: Kilosort2 output; 15 quality metrics; five region-specific logistic-regression classifiers (cortex, striatum, thalamus, midbrain, medulla) trained on manual Phy labels; units labelled **`good`** are used for all analyses. In the NWB files this classifier output is the `units.classification` column (`good` vs `unlabelled`), and `anno_name` holds the CCF annotation of classified units. The whitepaper explicitly argues that thresholding individual metrics is inadequate — hence using the provided classifier label is the faithful reproduction of their QC.\n- **Video markers**: DeepLabCut side-view tongue/jaw/nose; outliers detected by 5-sigma velocity threshold and imputed from nearby frames; when the tongue is occluded (in the mouth) the method paper sets tongue position to its mean value. Our decoder task instead requires an explicit \"not visible\" class (class 3), so occlusion is represented as its own category (detected via DLC likelihood).\n- **Region grouping** (reference preprocessing loop): ALM, Medulla, Midbrain, Striatum, Thalamus, Pons, Cerebellum, Hypothalamus, Hippocampus, Orbital, OtherCortex, Olfactory, CorticalSubplate, Pallidum — each split into left/right hemisphere with the CCF ML midline at 5,700 µm.\n\n### Curation Steps\n**Neuron curation rules (reference)**\n1. Keep only units with a CCF/histology annotation (units without histology are dropped).\n2. Keep only units labelled `good` by the QC classifier (25.9 % of Kilosort clusters).\n3. Method-paper analyses additionally drop neurons with mean firing rate < 2 Hz (for firing-rate *prediction* analyses) and brain areas with < 10 neurons per session. These are analysis-specific and are **not** appropriate for the decoding task here (they would discard most of the population available to the decoder), so they are not applied; documented in Step 5.\n\n**Trial curation rules (reference)**\n- \"regular\" trials = no early lick, no auto-water, no free water, no ignore (`correctness != -1`), and no photostimulation.\n- **Our decoder task requires early-lick, photostim, ignore and miss trials** (they are explicit decoder inputs/outputs), so these filters are relaxed; see Step 5.\n- Session inclusion criteria in the data paper (performance > 65 %, ≥ 50 correct left and right trials) are already satisfied by the published sessions.\n\n### Decoders Trained (reference accuracies)\n| Decoded variable | Accuracy |\n|---|---|\n| Choice from behavioral video, pre-sample epoch | AUC 0.51 ± 0.06 (n = 106 sessions) |\n| Choice from behavioral video, sample+delay epochs | AUC 0.66 ± 0.12 |\n| Choice from behavioral video, second half of response epoch | AUC 0.99 ± 0.01 |\n| Choice from single-neuron delay activity (AUC threshold for \"choice-modulated\") | AUC > 0.65 |\n| Uninstructed-movement type from single neurons | AUC > 0.65 threshold |\n\nImplication for our decoder: **choice** should be decodable near-perfectly after the go cue from population activity (video alone gives AUC 0.99); delay-epoch choice information is weaker. Outcome and early-lick should be decodable well above chance; tongue position (a directly observable movement) should be decodable well, since neural activity predicts video markers with high R² in the method paper.\n\n---\n\n## Step 4: Check for Consistency\n**Status**: COMPLETE\n\nI cross-checked the reference code (Step 1), the NWB data (Step 2) and the papers (Step 3). Unlabelled units also lack CCF annotations, so this simultaneously enforces the reference's \"must have histology\" rule. Result: 69,453 units (25.5 % of clusters) vs 69,943 (25.9 %) in the paper.\n2. **No additional firing-rate threshold**: the method paper's ≥ 2 Hz filter and its \"≥10 neurons per area per session\" rule apply to their neuron-wise *encoding* analyses; for population decoding, discarding low-rate neurons throws away usable signal and is not part of the dataset-level curation. Not applied (documented deviation).\n3. **Session curation**: drop sessions with 0 good units → exactly **173** sessions, matching the papers.\n4. **Trial curation**: drop `auto_water == 1` or `free_water == 1` trials (reward delivered independent of the animal's action ⇒ `outcome` is not a behavioural report), matching `get_regular_trial_mask`. **Keep** early-lick, ignore/miss and photostim trials, because the decoder task defines them as outputs/inputs; the reference excluded them only for its encoding analyses.\n5. **Alignment / window / binning**: go-cue aligned, −2.5 → +1.5 s, 80 × 50 ms non-overlapping bins, rates in Hz (counts / 0.05 s). Bin *i* covers [−2.5 + 0.05 i, −2.45 + 0.05 i); the value assigned to input/output time series uses the **bin centre**.\n6. **Unobserved time**: spikes exist only inside `[start_time, stop_time]` (= `obs_intervals`). 96.9 % of trials cover go−2.5 s, 84.4 % cover go+1.5 s (miss trials end early). Bins outside the recorded trial interval necessarily contain 0 spikes; these are kept as 0 (no extra information is available) and the fraction is reported in metadata.\n7. **Tongue visibility threshold**: `likelihood > 0.5`. The likelihood distribution is strongly bimodal (89 % < 0.1, 10 % > 0.9) so the exact threshold is immaterial.\n8. **Percentiles computed per session** over the *binned, visible* tongue-y values of the exported trials, so the resulting class frequencies are exactly 40 / 20 / 40 % of visible bins in each session.\n9. **Outputs are time-varying** (shape (4, 80)): per-trial variables are broadcast across bins, as recommended by the task description.\n10. **Brain regions carry hemisphere** (e.g. `left ALM`), as in the reference (`side_region`), with the CCF ML midline at 5,700 µm.\n\n### Planned Sanity Checks\n- [ ] 173 sessions, 28 subjects, 69,453 neurons after curation.\n- [ ] Per-coarse-region neuron totals reproduce paper values (striatum 7,664; rates = counts / 0.05 s.\n- `tone_onset_times()` — last `sample_start_times` at/ before the go cue per trial (handles early-lick epoch replays).\n- `photostim_binary()` — binary per-bin photostim indicator from `photostim_start/stop_times` events (bin counted as on if it overlaps the laser interval).\n- `bin_tongue()` — DLC side-camera tongue y averaged per 50 ms bin over frames with `likelihood > 0.5`, after 5σ velocity outlier rejection (method paper); NaN when no valid frame.\n- `discretize_tongue()` — per-session 40th/60th percentiles of the binned visible y → classes 0/1/2, NaN → 3.\n- `convert_session()` — loads one NWB with `pynwb`, curates units/trials, builds neural/input/output arrays and a `session_info` record with timings and QC statistics.\n- `make_processing_plots()` — 8-panel diagnostics per session (`--show-processing`): raw spike raster vs binned rates for one trial, population PSTH computed independently from raw spike times vs the converted neural mean, inputs vs raw event times, raw tongue trace vs binned values and percentile thresholds, resulting discrete tongue classes, per-trial outputs, tongue-class time course.\n- `main()` — parallel over sessions (`ProcessPoolExecutor`, default 16 workers), assembles the target dictionary, writes the pickle, prints summary statistics.\n\nEfficiency:\n- Spike times are read once per unit; binning is vectorised with `searchsorted` over concatenated bin edges (0.16 s/session for ~450 neurons × 400 trials).\n- Unit → electrode lookup uses the `VectorIndex` arrays directly instead of per-unit `units['electrodes'][i]` DataFrame construction (~100× faster; verified to give identical electrode ids).\n- Video tracking arrays are read once per session and binned with `np.bincount`.\n- Sessions are processed in parallel (16 workers), so the wall-clock cost is dominated by pickling the ~10 GB result.\n\nIssue found and fixed during development: **trials with no ephys at all**. In 100 sessions some trials (4.35 % overall; 2 sessions where the probes stop long before the behaviour: 376/582 and 321/480 trials) contain zero spikes from *every* good unit over the whole trial. NWB does not flag them (`is_good_trials` is all-True and `obs_intervals` simply mirror the trials table). Such trials are excluded as invalid data periods.\n\n---\n\n## Step 7: Sample Conversion and Validation\n**Status**: COMPLETE\n\n`python -u /app/convert_data.py /app/sample_data.pkl --sample --show-processing` → `/app/conversion_sample_out.txt`;\n`python -u /app/train_decoder.py /app/sample_data.pkl --verify-only` → `/app/verification_sample_out.txt` (**no errors, no warnings**).\n\n### Sample Statistics (2 sessions of mouse 440956 / SC015)\n| Statistic | Value |\n|-----------|-------|\n| Sessions | 2 |\n| Neurons (total) | 834 |\n| Neurons / session | 459, 375 |","numLines":260,"startLine":1,"totalLines":520}}}

How is the per-trial `neural` data aligned to the event described in the `instructions`?\n\ni. All NWB times (spike times, event timestamps, camera timestamps) are on the same session-absolute clock, so no resampling or per-stream offset correction is required. Alignment is done by adding the fixed go-cue-relative edge grid to each trial's go-cue time (`go_start_times`, one per trial) and binning the raw spikes against those absolute edges. `metadata['temporal_alignment_event']` records the choice.\n\nii.\n```python\nOFF_START = -2.5          # s relative to go cue\nOFF_END = 1.5             # s relative to go cue\nNBINS = int(round((OFF_END - OFF_START) / BIN_SIZE))   # 80\nBIN_EDGES_REL = OFF_START + BIN_SIZE * np.arange(NBINS + 1)\nBIN_CENTERS_REL = BIN_EDGES_REL[:-1] + BIN_SIZE / 2\n```\n\n```python\n        go = np.asarray(be['go_start_times'].timestamps[:], dtype=float)\n```\n\n```python\n    edges = (go_times[:, None] + BIN_EDGES_REL[None, :]).ravel()\n    out = np.empty((len(spike_times_list), ntr, NBINS), dtype=np.float32)\n    for k, st in enumerate(spike_times_list):\n        idx = np.searchsorted(st, edges).reshape(ntr, NBINS + 1)\n        out[k] = np.diff(idx, axis=1)\n```\n\n```python\n            'temporal_alignment_event': 'auditory go cue onset (BehavioralEvents go_start_times)',\n            'off_start': OFF_START,\n            'off_end': OFF_END,\n```\n\niii. What is the temporal resolution (time bin size) of the converted data? Is any temporal rebinning applied?\n\ni. 50 ms, giving 80 non-overlapping bins spanning −2.5 s to +1.5 s relative to the go cue, identical for every trial and every session. The grid is defined once at module level (81 relative edges, 80 relative centres) and reused everywhere, so the neural, input and output streams all share the same bins. There is no rebinning of an already-binned product: spikes are binned once directly from raw spike times, and the video (native dt = 3.4 ms) is averaged once into the same 50 ms grid. The bin width is exported as `metadata['time_bin_size'] = 50.0` (ms), with the bin centres also stored.\n\nii.\n```python\nBIN_SIZE = 0.05           # s, 50 ms bins (decoder task specification)\nOFF_START = -2.5          # s relative to go cue\nOFF_END = 1.5             # s relative to go cue\nNBINS = int(round((OFF_END - OFF_START) / BIN_SIZE))   # 80\nBIN_EDGES_REL = OFF_START + BIN_SIZE * np.arange(NBINS + 1)\nBIN_CENTERS_REL = BIN_EDGES_REL[:-1] + BIN_SIZE / 2\n```\n\n```python\n            'time_bin_size': BIN_SIZE * 1000.0,\n            'time_bin_size_units': 'ms',\n            ...\n            'bin_centers_re_go_cue_s': BIN_CENTERS_REL.tolist(),\n```\n\niii. CONVERSION_NOTES.md Step 3: the method paper \"binned spikes into firing rates with a bin width of 40 ms and a stride of 3.4 ms\", but \"Our task specifies **50 ms bins**, which we implement as non-overlapping 50 ms bins giving rates in Hz (80 bins over −2.5→+1.5 s)\". Step 4: \"Task specifies **50 ms bins** → non-overlapping 50 ms bins, rates in Hz (counts/0.05 s), 80 bins for −2.5→+1.5 s\", and Step 5 Key Decision 5: \"Bin *i* covers [−2.5 + 0.05 i, −2.45 + 0.05 i); the value assigned to input/output time series uses the **bin centre**.\" Step 10 Check 5 verifies the half-open-bin convention: \"`searchsorted` with `side='left'` makes bins half-open, so no spike is counted twice — verified by summing counts over bins and comparing with a direct count in [−2.5, 1.5) (equal).\" The verifier confirms `T: min 80, max 80` over the whole dataset.\n\n## 3-a. What variables in the raw data is `input` *Time from tone onset in seconds* derived from?\n\ni. From `BehavioralEvents/sample_start_times` (the onsets of the sample/tone epoch), `trials.start_time` (used to assign each sample event to a trial), and `go_start_times`. For each trial the tone taken is the **last** `sample_start` that belongs to that trial and occurs at or before its go cue, because an early lick replays the sample epoch and a trial can therefore carry several sample-start events.\n\nii.\n```python\ndef tone_onset_times(sample_starts, trial_starts, go_times):\n    \"\"\"Last sample(tone)-epoch start at or before the go cue, for each trial.\n\n    Early licking triggers a replay of the sample/delay epoch, so a trial can contain several\n    `sample_start_times`; the *last* one before the go cue is the tone the animal responded to.\n    \"\"\"\n    ntr = len(go_times)\n    out = np.full(ntr, np.nan)\n    if len(sample_starts):\n        tidx = np.searchsorted(trial_starts, sample_starts, side='right') - 1\n        ok = (tidx >= 0) & (tidx < ntr)\n        tidx, ev = tidx[ok], sample_starts[ok]\n        ok2 = ev <= go_times[tidx]\n        tidx, ev = tidx[ok2], ev[ok2]\n        order = np.argsort(ev, kind='stable')          # ascending -> last write wins\n        out[tidx[order]] = ev[order]\n    return out\n```\n\n```python\n        sample_starts = np.asarray(be['sample_start_times'].timestamps[:], dtype=float)\n        ...\n        tone = tone_onset_times(sample_starts, trial_start, go)[kidx]\n```\n\niii. CONVERSION_NOTES.md Step 2: \"`sample_*` and `delay_*` have **more** events than trials because early licking triggers a **replay** of the sample/delay epoch (confirmed: extra sample events occur only in `early` trials)\"; \"Last `sample_start` before the go cue is ~1.85–1.95 s before the go cue (tone onset); this matches the paper's sample epoch start at −1.85 s and 1.2 s delay.\" Step 4: \"Early-lick trials trigger epoch *replays*, so the **last** sample start before the go cue is the tone the animal actually used.\" Step 5 mapping: \"median = 1.85 s before the go cue in every session; using the **last** sample start handles early-lick replays.\" The verifier reports the median tone onset at exactly −1.850 s re go cue across all 173 sessions.\n\n## 3-b. What processing is involved in computing `input` *Time from tone onset in seconds*?\n\ni. The tone time is expressed relative to the trial's go cue (`tone_rel_go = tone − go`, typically ≈ −1.85 s), and each bin's value is its go-cue-relative centre minus that offset, i.e. seconds elapsed since tone onset at that bin centre. The result is a continuous, time-varying `float32` row of length 80, stored as row 0 of the per-trial `(2, 80)` input array. Values run from ≈ −0.65 s (bin before the tone on a normal trial) upward; the full converted range is [−1.525, 5.936] s, with the large values coming from early-lick replay trials where the final tone is close to the go cue but earlier bins reach back before an earlier replay.\n\nii.\n```python\n        tone = tone_onset_times(sample_starts, trial_start, go)[kidx]\n        tone_rel_go = tone - go[kidx]                             # negative, ~ -1.85 s\n        # time since tone onset at each bin centre (s)\n        time_from_tone = (BIN_CENTERS_REL[None, :] - tone_rel_go[:, None]).astype(np.float32)\n```\n\n```python\n        input_trials = [np.stack([time_from_tone[i], photostim[i]]).astype(np.float32)\n                        for i in range(ntr)]\n```\n\niii. CONVERSION_NOTES.md Step 5 mapping table: \"last `sample_start_times` ≤ go cue, per trial → `input[0]` = `time_from_tone_onset_s`; bin-center time − tone-onset time (seconds), continuous, time-varying (80 values)\". Step 5 Key Decision 5 fixes the bin-centre convention for input/output time series. Planned sanity check: \"`input[0]` (time from tone onset) ≈ −0.65 … 3.35 s with median tone onset at −1.85 s re go cue\"; Step 9 reports the achieved range [−1.53, 11.9] s (the max in the pickle summary is 5.936 s; the verifier reports 11.9 s) and explains it as \"long values come from early-lick replay trials\". Step 10 Check 2 verified the full 80-bin time-from-tone vector against independently recomputed values for 4 random trials in each of 4 sessions.\n\n## 3-c. How is the `input` *Time from tone onset in seconds* aligned with the neural data?\n\ni. It is constructed *on* the neural bin grid: the same module-level `BIN_CENTERS_REL` array that defines the 80 spike bins is what is shifted by the tone-to-go-cue gap. Bin *k* of the input therefore refers to exactly the interval whose spikes are in bin *k* of `neural`, by construction — no interpolation or index matching is needed.\n\nii.\n```python\nBIN_EDGES_REL = OFF_START + BIN_SIZE * np.arange(NBINS + 1)\nBIN_CENTERS_REL = BIN_EDGES_REL[:-1] + BIN_SIZE / 2\n```\n\n```python\n    edges = (go_times[:, None] + BIN_EDGES_REL[None, :]).ravel()   # neural bins\n```\n\n```python\n        time_from_tone = (BIN_CENTERS_REL[None, :] - tone_rel_go[:, None]).astype(np.float32)\n```\n\niii. CONVERSION_NOTES.md Step 5 mapping table: \"`BehavioralEvents['photostim_start_times' / 'photostim_stop_times'].timestamps` → `input[1]` = `photostim_on` … `stimulation[:,2:] -= gocue_time` (reference stores on/off times re go cue) … cross-checked against the `trials.photostim_onset/power/duration` columns.\" The AI verified the stimulation parameters against the papers (Step 4: \"18,588/94,990 trials (19.6 %) at 5.5 mW, always 0.5 s; onset −1.2 s or −0.5 s re go cue\" vs \"~25 % randomly interleaved trials, 5 mW/hemisphere, last 0.5 s of delay\"; \"Stim always **ends before the go cue** ✓ (max stim end = go − 0.499 s)\"). Each laser event is assigned to the trial whose `start_time` last precedes it; the on/off times are converted to go-cue-relative seconds; a bin is set to 1 if the stimulation interval **overlaps** the bin interval (`bin_start < off` and `bin_end > on`), 0 otherwise. Trials with no laser event stay all-zero. A defensive swap handles any entry where the stop time precedes the start time. Stored as `float32` row 1 of the `(2, 80)` input array.\n\nii.\n```python\ndef photostim_binary(stim_on, stim_off, trial_starts, go_times):\n    \"\"\"(n_trials, NBINS) binary array: is photostimulation on during this bin?\"\"\"\n    ntr = len(go_times)\n    ps = np.zeros((ntr, NBINS), dtype=np.float32)\n    if len(stim_on) == 0:\n        return ps\n    tidx = np.searchsorted(trial_starts, stim_on, side='right') - 1\n    for i, on, off in zip(tidx, stim_on, stim_off):\n        if i < 0 or i >= ntr:\n            continue\n        on_rel, off_rel = on - go_times[i], off - go_times[i]\n        if off_rel < on_rel:                      # guard against corrupt entries\n            on_rel, off_rel = off_rel, on_rel\n        # a bin is 'on' if the stimulation interval overlaps the bin\n        overlap = (BIN_EDGES_REL[:-1] < off_rel) & (BIN_EDGES_REL[1:] > on_rel)\n        ps[i, overlap] = 1.0\n    return ps\n```\n\niii. CONVERSION_NOTES.md Step 5 mapping table: \"1 if the 50 ms bin overlaps [stim_on, stim_off] (times re go cue), else 0; binary time-varying\". The instructions require \"Whether **photostimulation** is on at every time point (discrete, time-varying)\" and \"If an input is a time such as onset of some stimulus, represent it as a binary time series\", which the AI cites in Step 5 Key Decision 9. Planned sanity check: \"`input[1]` on only before the go cue, total duration 0.5 s per stim trial, and 0 for all non-stim trials\" — confirmed in Step 9 (20.0 % of trials stimulated; laser always ends before the go cue) and in the processing plots (\"Photostim input turns on exactly over the raw `photostim_start/stop` shading and always ends before the go cue\"). Four steps:\n1. **Visibility mask** — frames with `likelihood > 0.5` count as visible (the tracker still emits a position when the tongue is retracted).\n2. **Outlier rejection** — among the visible frames, the inter-frame velocity `dy/dt` is computed and frames following a jump larger than 5 σ are invalidated, following the method paper's 5-sigma velocity outlier rule.\n3. **Binning** — for each trial, the valid frames inside `[go − 2.5, go + 1.5)` are averaged (via `np.bincount` sum/count) into the same 80 × 50 ms bins; a bin with no valid frame is left `NaN`.\n4. **Discretisation** — per session, the 40th and 60th percentiles of *all finite binned values* are taken and each bin is assigned class 0/1/2; `NaN` bins become class 3, \"not visible\".\n\nNo mean-imputation is done for occluded frames (the method paper imputes the mean), because the task requires an explicit \"not visible\" category.\n\nii.\n```python\nTONGUE_LIK_THRESH = 0.5   # DeepLabCut likelihood above which the tongue is 'visible'\nVELOCITY_SIGMA = 5.0      # 5-sigma velocity outlier rejection (method paper)\n```\n\n```python\ndef bin_tongue(ts, y, lik, go_times):\n    \"\"\"Mean visible tongue y-position per 50 ms bin, NaN where the tongue is not visible.\"\"\"\n    ntr = len(go_times)\n    visible = lik > TONGUE_LIK_THRESH\n    valid = visible.copy()\n    if visible.sum() > 10:\n        iv = np.where(visible)[0]\n        dy = np.diff(y[iv]) / np.maximum(np.diff(ts[iv]), 1e-6)\n        s = np.std(dy)\n        if s > 0:\n            bad = np.abs(dy) > VELOCITY_SIGMA * s\n            # a large jump invalidates the frame after the jump\n            valid[iv[1:][bad]] = False\n    res = np.full((ntr, NBINS), np.nan, dtype=np.float32)\n    t0 = go_times + OFF_START\n    lo = np.searchsorted(ts, t0)\n    hi = np.searchsorted(ts, go_times + OFF_END)\n    for i in range(ntr):\n        a, b = lo[i], hi[i]\n        if b <= a:\n            continue\n        tsel = ts[a:b]\n        vsel = valid[a:b]\n        if not vsel.any():\n            continue\n        bi = np.floor((tsel[vsel] - t0[i]) / BIN_SIZE).astype(int)\n        np.clip(bi, 0, NBINS - 1, out=bi)\n        cnt = np.bincount(bi, minlength=NBINS)\n        sm = np.bincount(bi, weights=y[a:b][vsel], minlength=NBINS)\n        nz = cnt > 0\n        res[i, nz] = (sm[nz] / cnt[nz]).astype(np.float32)\n    return res\n```\n\niii. CONVERSION_NOTES.md Step 3: \"**Video markers**: DeepLabCut side-view tongue/jaw/nose; outliers detected by 5-sigma velocity threshold and imputed from nearby frames; when the tongue is occluded (in the mouth) the method paper sets tongue position to its mean value. Our decoder task instead requires an explicit 'not visible' class (class 3), so occlusion is represented as its own category (detected via DLC likelihood).\" Step 5 Key Decision 7: \"**Tongue visibility threshold**: `likelihood > 0.5`. The likelihood distribution is strongly bimodal (89 % < 0.1, 10 % > 0.9) so the exact threshold is immaterial.\" Step 5 Key Decision 8: \"**Percentiles computed per session** over the *binned, visible* tongue-y values of the exported trials, so the resulting class frequencies are exactly 40 / 20 / 40 % of visible bins in each session.\" (Note: the Step 5 mapping table says \"median y of frames in that bin\" while the code, its docstring, Step 6 and the README all say the bin **mean**; the code computes the mean.) Step 10 Check 2 recomputed the complete tongue class matrix from raw DLC data for 4 sessions with independent code: \"✓ agreement 1.0000\".\n\n## 8-c. How is `output` *Tongue y-position* thresholded into categories?\n\ni. Per session, the 40th and 60th percentiles of the finite (visible) binned y-values are computed and used as the two class edges: `y < p40 → 0`, `p40 ≤ y ≤ p60 → 1`, `y > p60 → 2`; `NaN` (no visible frame in the bin) → `3`. The percentiles and the visible fraction are recorded per session in `session_info` (`tongue_p40`, `tongue_p60`, `frac_bins_tongue_visible`). Because the percentiles are taken over exactly the quantity being discretised, the visible bins split exactly 40/20/40 within each session; over the whole dataset the classes come out 0.101 / 0.050 / 0.101 / 0.749.\n\nii.\n```python\ndef discretize_tongue(y_binned):\n    \"\"\"Per-session discretisation of tongue y into 4 classes (task specification).\"\"\"\n    vis = np.isfinite(y_binned)\n    cls = np.full(y_binned.shape, 3, dtype=np.int64)     # 3 = not visible\n    if vis.sum() > 0:\n        p40, p60 = np.percentile(y_binned[vis], [40, 60])\n        v = y_binned[vis]\n        c = np.where(v < p40, 0, np.where(v <= p60, 1, 2))\n        cls[vis] = c\n    else:\n        p40 = p60 = np.nan\n    return cls, float(p40), float(p60)\n```\n\n```python\nOUTPUT_VALUES = [\n    ...\n    ['<40th pct', '40-60th pct', '>60th pct', 'not visible'],\n]\n```\n\niii. Directly from the Decoder Task specification (\"0: < 40th percentile of y-position over the session; 1: 40th to 60th percentile; 2: > 60th percentile; 3: not visible\"), recorded in CONVERSION_NOTES.md Step 5 Key Decision 8 and in the exported metadata: \"per-session percentiles (40th, 60th) of the binned, visible tongue y-position; bins with no frame of likelihood > 0.5 (or only 5-sigma velocity outliers) are class 3 = 'not visible'\". Planned sanity check: \"Tongue class distribution: within-session visible bins split 40/20/40; class 3 dominates before the go cue and drops after it\" — confirmed both numerically (Step 9) and visually in the `--show-processing` panels (2,0), (2,1) and (3,1), which draw the p40/p60 lines over the raw trace and plot the class time course.\n\n## 8-d. How is `output` *Tongue y-position* aligned with the neural data?\n\ni. The camera timestamps are on the same session-absolute clock as the spikes and the go cues, so alignment is a direct index lookup: `np.searchsorted` on the camera timestamps finds the frame range `[go − 2.5, go + 1.5)` for each trial, and each frame is assigned to bin `floor((t − (go − 2.5)) / 0.05)` — the identical go-cue-relative grid used for the firing rates (indices clipped into `[0, 79]` to guard floating-point edge cases). CONVERSION_NOTES.md Step 5 mapping table: \"`units.spike_times` (session clock) for units with `classification == 'good'` → `neural[session][trial]` (n_neurons, 80)\". How is the `neural` data processed?\n\ni. Spike times are converted to per-bin firing rates in Hz. For each good unit, the absolute bin edges of *all* trials are built as one flat array (`go[:, None] + BIN_EDGES_REL[None, :]`), a single `np.searchsorted` gives the running spike count at every edge, and `np.diff` along the bin axis converts those running counts into a spike count per bin. Counts are divided by the 50 ms bin width to give Hz, stored `float32`. No smoothing, baseline subtraction, normalisation, or firing-rate threshold is applied.\n\nii.\n```python\ndef bin_spikes(spike_times_list, go_times):\n    \"\"\"Spike counts -> firing rate (Hz) in non-overlapping BIN_SIZE bins around the go cue.\n\n    Analogue of the reference `sliding_histogram(..., rate=True)` with stride == bin width.\n    \"\"\"\n    ntr = len(go_times)\n    edges = (go_times[:, None] + BIN_EDGES_REL[None, :]).ravel()\n    out = np.empty((len(spike_times_list), ntr, NBINS), dtype=np.float32)\n    for k, st in enumerate(spike_times_list):\n        idx = np.searchsorted(st, edges).reshape(ntr, NBINS + 1)\n        out[k] = np.diff(idx, axis=1)\n    out /= np.float32(BIN_SIZE)\n    return out\n```\n\n```python\n        neural_trials = [np.ascontiguousarray(fr[:, i, :]) for i in range(ntr)]\n```\n\niii. CONVERSION_NOTES.md Step 1: the reference `sliding_histogram(spikeTimes, begin, end, bin_width, stride, rate=True)` \"returns … firing **rates** (counts / bin_width)\"; Step 6: \"`bin_spikes()` — vectorised analogue of the reference `sliding_histogram(..., rate=True)` with stride = width = 50 ms: per neuron a single `np.searchsorted` over all trial-bin edges, then `np.diff`; rates = counts / 0.05 s.\" Step 5 Key Decision 2 explains that the method paper's ≥ 2 Hz firing-rate filter and \"≥ 10 neurons per area per session\" rule are *not* applied: \"these apply to their neuron-wise *encoding* analyses; for population decoding, discarding low-rate neurons throws away usable signal and is not part of the dataset-level curation.\" The units of the result (Hz) are recorded in metadata (`'neural_units': 'firing rate (Hz), spike counts per 50 ms bin / 0.05 s'`).\n\n## 2-c. What is the temporal resolution (time bin size) of the converted data? Is any temporal rebinning applied?\n\ni. 50 ms, giving 80 non-overlapping bins spanning −2.5 s to +1.5 s relative to the go cue, identical for every trial and every session. What variables in the raw data is `input` *Time from tone onset in seconds* derived from?\n\ni. From `BehavioralEvents/sample_start_times` (the onsets of the sample/tone epoch), `trials.start_time` (used to assign each sample event to a trial), and `go_start_times`. For each trial the tone taken is the **last** `sample_start` that belongs to that trial and occurs at or before its go cue, because an early lick replays the sample epoch and a trial can therefore carry several sample-start events.\n\nii.\n```python\ndef tone_onset_times(sample_starts, trial_starts, go_times):\n    \"\"\"Last sample(tone)-epoch start at or before the go cue, for each trial.\n\n    Early licking triggers a replay of the sample/delay epoch, so a trial can contain several\n    `sample_start_times`; the *last* one before the go cue is the tone the animal responded to.\n    \"\"\"\n    ntr = len(go_times)\n    out = np.full(ntr, np.nan)\n    if len(sample_starts):\n        tidx = np.searchsorted(trial_starts, sample_starts, side='right') - 1\n        ok = (tidx >= 0) & (tidx < ntr)\n        tidx, ev = tidx[ok], sample_starts[ok]\n        ok2 = ev <= go_times[tidx]\n        tidx, ev = tidx[ok2], ev[ok2]\n        order = np.argsort(ev, kind='stable')          # ascending -> last write wins\n        out[tidx[order]] = ev[order]\n    return out\n```\n\n```python\n        sample_starts = np.asarray(be['sample_start_times'].timestamps[:], dtype=float)\n        ...\n        tone = tone_onset_times(sample_starts, trial_start, go)[kidx]\n```\n\niii. What processing is involved in computing `input` *Time from tone onset in seconds*?\n\ni. The result is a continuous, time-varying `float32` row of length 80, stored as row 0 of the per-trial `(2, 80)` input array. Values run from ≈ −0.65 s (bin before the tone on a normal trial) upward; the full converted range is [−1.525, 5.936] s, with the large values coming from early-lick replay trials where the final tone is close to the go cue but earlier bins reach back before an earlier replay.\n\nii.\n```python\n        tone = tone_onset_times(sample_starts, trial_start, go)[kidx]\n        tone_rel_go = tone - go[kidx]                             # negative, ~ -1.85 s\n        # time since tone onset at each bin centre (s)\n        time_from_tone = (BIN_CENTERS_REL[None, :] - tone_rel_go[:, None]).astype(np.float32)\n```\n\n```python\n        input_trials = [np.stack([time_from_tone[i], photostim[i]]).astype(np.float32)\n                        for i in range(ntr)]\n```\n\niii. CONVERSION_NOTES.md Step 5 mapping table: \"`BehavioralEvents['photostim_start_times' / 'photostim_stop_times'].timestamps` → `input[1]` = `photostim_on` … `stimulation[:,2:] -= gocue_time` (reference stores on/off times re go cue) … cross-checked against the `trials.photostim_onset/power/duration` columns.\" The AI verified the stimulation parameters against the papers (Step 4: \"18,588/94,990 trials (19.6 %) at 5.5 mW, always 0.5 s; onset −1.2 s or −0.5 s re go cue\" vs \"~25 % randomly interleaved trials, 5 mW/hemisphere, last 0.5 s of delay\"; \"Stim always **ends before the go cue** ✓ (max stim end = go − 0.499 s)\"). The conversion is correct; no change needed.\"\n\n## 4-b. What processing is involved in computing `input` *Photostimulation*?\n\ni. A binary, time-varying trace on the same 80-bin grid. Each laser event is assigned to the trial whose `start_time` last precedes it; the on/off times are converted to go-cue-relative seconds; a bin is set to 1 if the stimulation interval **overlaps** the bin interval (`bin_start < off` and `bin_end > on`), 0 otherwise. Trials with no laser event stay all-zero. A defensive swap handles any entry where the stop time precedes the start time. Stored as `float32` row 1 of the `(2, 80)` input array.\n\nii.\n```python\ndef photostim_binary(stim_on, stim_off, trial_starts, go_times):\n    \"\"\"(n_trials, NBINS) binary array: is photostimulation on during this bin?\"\"\"\n    ntr = len(go_times)\n    ps = np.zeros((ntr, NBINS), dtype=np.float32)\n    if len(stim_on) == 0:\n        return ps\n    tidx = np.searchsorted(trial_starts, stim_on, side='right') - 1\n    for i, on, off in zip(tidx, stim_on, stim_off):\n        if i < 0 or i >= ntr:\n            continue\n        on_rel, off_rel = on - go_times[i], off - go_times[i]\n        if off_rel < on_rel:                      # guard against corrupt entries\n            on_rel, off_rel = off_rel, on_rel\n        # a bin is 'on' if the stimulation interval overlaps the bin\n        overlap = (BIN_EDGES_REL[:-1] < off_rel) & (BIN_EDGES_REL[1:] > on_rel)\n        ps[i, overlap] = 1.0\n    return ps\n```\n\niii. CONVERSION_NOTES.md Step 5 mapping table: \"1 if the 50 ms bin overlaps [stim_on, stim_off] (times re go cue), else 0; binary time-varying\". The instructions require \"Whether **photostimulation** is on at every time point (discrete, time-varying)\" and \"If an input is a time such as onset of some stimulus, represent it as a binary time series\", which the AI cites in Step 5 Key Decision 9. Planned sanity check: \"`input[1]` on only before the go cue, total duration 0.5 s per stim trial, and 0 for all non-stim trials\" — confirmed in Step 9 (20.0 % of trials stimulated; laser always ends before the go cue) and in the processing plots (\"Photostim input turns on exactly over the raw `photostim_start/stop` shading and always ends before the go cue\"). Step 10 Check 2 rebuilt the complete `(n_trials × 80)` photostim matrix from the raw events for 4 sessions with independent code and matched it exactly.\n\n## 4-c. How is the `input` *Photostimulation* aligned with the neural data?\n\ni. By converting the laser on/off times into go-cue-relative seconds (`on − go[i]`, `off − go[i]`) and comparing them against the same `BIN_EDGES_REL` array that defines the spike bins. Bin *k* of `photostim_on` therefore covers precisely the interval of bin *k* of `neural`.\n\nii.\n```python\n        on_rel, off_rel = on - go_times[i], off - go_times[i]\n        ...\n        overlap = (BIN_EDGES_REL[:-1] < off_rel) & (BIN_EDGES_REL[1:] > on_rel)\n```\n\niii. CONVERSION_NOTES.md Step 2: \"`nwb.acquisition['BehavioralTimeSeries']`: DeepLabCut side-view (`Camera0_side_`) tracking `JawTracking`, `NoseTracking`, `TongueTracking` (all 174 sessions) … Each has `data` of shape (n_frames, 3) = (x, y, likelihood) and explicit `timestamps` in session time with **dt = 0.0034 s** (identical in all 174 sessions).\" This is the only tongue measurement in the file and is present in every session. Step 1 identifies the reference counterpart `Sherlock/align_markers.py::align_markers_between_lims`, which aligns the same DLC side-camera markers (`nose/tongue/jaw/whisker` x,y) to the go cue at dt = 0.0034 s. Step 3 confirms the cameras run at 300 Hz per the data paper.\n\n## 8-b. What processing is involved in computing `output` *Tongue y-position*?\n\ni. Four steps:\n1. **Visibility mask** — frames with `likelihood > 0.5` count as visible (the tracker still emits a position when the tongue is retracted).\n2. **Outlier rejection** — among the visible frames, the inter-frame velocity `dy/dt` is computed and frames following a jump larger than 5 σ are invalidated, following the method paper's 5-sigma velocity outlier rule.\n3. **Binning** — for each trial, the valid frames inside `[go − 2.5, go + 1.5)` are averaged (via `np.bincount` sum/count) into the same 80 × 50 ms bins; a bin with no valid frame is left `NaN`.\n4. **Discretisation** — per session, the 40th and 60th percentiles of *all finite binned values* are taken and each bin is assigned class 0/1/2; `NaN` bins become class 3, \"not visible\".\n\nNo mean-imputation is done for occluded frames (the method paper imputes the mean), because the task requires an explicit \"not visible\" category.\n\nii.\n```python\nTONGUE_LIK_THRESH = 0.5   # DeepLabCut likelihood above which the tongue is 'visible'\nVELOCITY_SIGMA = 5.0      # 5-sigma velocity outlier rejection (method paper)\n```\n\n```python\ndef bin_tongue(ts, y, lik, go_times):\n    \"\"\"Mean visible tongue y-position per 50 ms bin, NaN where the tongue is not visible.\"\"\"\n    ntr = len(go_times)\n    visible = lik > TONGUE_LIK_THRESH\n    valid = visible.copy()\n    if visible.sum() > 10:\n        iv = np.where(visible)[0]\n        dy = np.diff(y[iv]) / np.maximum(np.diff(ts[iv]), 1e-6)\n        s = np.std(dy)\n        if s > 0:\n            bad = np.abs(dy) > VELOCITY_SIGMA * s\n            # a large jump invalidates the frame after the jump\n            valid[iv[1:][bad]] = False\n    res = np.full((ntr, NBINS), np.nan, dtype=np.float32)\n    t0 = go_times + OFF_START\n    lo = np.searchsorted(ts, t0)\n    hi = np.searchsorted(ts, go_times + OFF_END)\n    for i in range(ntr):\n        a, b = lo[i], hi[i]\n        if b <= a:\n            continue\n        tsel = ts[a:b]\n        vsel = valid[a:b]\n        if not vsel.any():\n            continue\n        bi = np.floor((tsel[vsel] - t0[i]) / BIN_SIZE).astype(int)\n        np.clip(bi, 0, NBINS - 1, out=bi)\n        cnt = np.bincount(bi, minlength=NBINS)\n        sm = np.bincount(bi, weights=y[a:b][vsel], minlength=NBINS)\n        nz = cnt > 0\n        res[i, nz] = (sm[nz] / cnt[nz]).astype(np.float32)\n    return res\n```\n\niii. CONVERSION_NOTES.md Step 3: \"**Video markers**: DeepLabCut side-view tongue/jaw/nose; outliers detected by 5-sigma velocity threshold and imputed from nearby frames; when the tongue is occluded (in the mouth) the method paper sets tongue position to its mean value. Our decoder task instead requires an explicit 'not visible' class (class 3), so occlusion is represented as its own category (detected via DLC likelihood).\" Step 5 Key Decision 7: \"**Tongue visibility threshold**: `likelihood > 0.5`. The likelihood distribution is strongly bimodal (89 % < 0.1, 10 % > 0.9) so the exact threshold is immaterial.\" Step 5 Key Decision 8: \"**Percentiles computed per session** over the *binned, visible* tongue-y values of the exported trials, so the resulting class frequencies are exactly 40 / 20 / 40 % of visible bins in each session.\" (Note: the Step 5 mapping table says \"median y of frames in that bin\" while the code, its docstring, Step 6 and the README all say the bin **mean**; the code computes the mean.) Step 10 Check 2 recomputed the complete tongue class matrix from raw DLC data for 4 sessions with independent code: \"✓ agreement 1.0000\".\n\n## 8-c. How is `output` *Tongue y-position* thresholded into categories?\n\ni. Per session, the 40th and 60th percentiles of the finite (visible) binned y-values are computed and used as the two class edges: `y < p40 → 0`, `p40 ≤ y ≤ p60 → 1`, `y > p60 → 2`; `NaN` (no visible frame in the bin) → `3`. The percentiles and the visible fraction are recorded per session in `session_info` (`tongue_p40`, `tongue_p60`, `frac_bins_tongue_visible`). Because the percentiles are taken over exactly the quantity being discretised, the visible bins split exactly 40/20/40 within each session; over the whole dataset the classes come out 0.101 / 0.050 / 0.101 / 0.749.\n\nii.\n```python\ndef discretize_tongue(y_binned):\n    \"\"\"Per-session discretisation of tongue y into 4 classes (task specification).\"\"\"\n    vis = np.isfinite(y_binned)\n    cls = np.full(y_binned.shape, 3, dtype=np.int64)     # 3 = not visible\n    if vis.sum() > 0:\n        p40, p60 = np.percentile(y_binned[vis], [40, 60])\n        v = y_binned[vis]\n        c = np.where(v < p40, 0, np.where(v <= p60, 1, 2))\n        cls[vis] = c\n    else:\n        p40 = p60 = np.nan\n    return cls, float(p40), float(p60)\n```\n\n```python\nOUTPUT_VALUES = [\n    ...\n    ['<40th pct', '40-60th pct', '>60th pct', 'not visible'],\n]\n```\n\niii. Directly from the Decoder Task specification (\"0: < 40th percentile of y-position over the session; 1: 40th to 60th percentile; 2: > 60th percentile; 3: not visible\"), recorded in CONVERSION_NOTES.md Step 5 Key Decision 8 and in the exported metadata: \"per-session percentiles (40th, 60th) of the binned, visible tongue y-position; bins with no frame of likelihood > 0.5 (or only 5-sigma velocity outliers) are class 3 = 'not visible'\". Planned sanity check: \"Tongue class distribution: within-session visible bins split 40/20/40; class 3 dominates before the go cue and drops after it\" — confirmed both numerically (Step 9) and visually in the `--show-processing` panels (2,0), (2,1) and (3,1), which draw the p40/p60 lines over the raw trace and plot the class time course.\n\n## 8-d. How is `output` *Tongue y-position* aligned with the neural data?\n\ni. No interpolation or resampling is applied. Video is trial-gated (each trial's segment starts at that trial's `start_time`), so bins before the trial's video start simply contain no frames and become class 3.\n\nii.\n```python\n    t0 = go_times + OFF_START\n    lo = np.searchsorted(ts, t0)\n    hi = np.searchsorted(ts, go_times + OFF_END)\n    for i in range(ntr):\n        a, b = lo[i], hi[i]\n        if b <= a:\n            continue\n        ...\n        bi = np.floor((tsel[vsel] - t0[i]) / BIN_SIZE).astype(int)\n        np.clip(bi, 0, NBINS - 1, out=bi)\n```\n\niii. CONVERSION_NOTES.md Step 2 established that the tracking series carries \"explicit `timestamps` in session time … segmented per trial: each trial's video segment starts exactly at that trial's `start_time`\", and Step 1 records that the reference's `align_markers_between_lims` aligns the same markers to the go cue.
