How are minor mistakes in the data, e.g. missing data, handled?\n\ni. Five cases, each handled explicitly and documented:\n\n- **Session never quality-controlled** (`classification` is NaN for all units): `.astype(str)` turns the non-string entries into `'nan'`, no unit matches `'good'`, and the session is dropped with a printed reason. This is the single dropped session, `SC017_20190216_162508_s4`, and dropping it brings the count to the published 173.\n- **Trials with no ephys** (acquisition gaps / probes stopped early): detected as zero total spikes across all good units in the window and removed (see 1-e); a session is dropped if fewer than 2 trials remain.\n- **Trials shorter than the analysis window**: *not* dropped. Spikes are only recorded within `[start_time, stop_time]`, so 3.2 % of trials start after go − 2.5 s and 15.6 % end before go + 1.5 s; the uncovered bins are genuinely 0 spikes and are left as 0, with the per-session coverage fractions stored in `session_info` (`frac_trials_observed_at_start/end`) and the situation described in `metadata['notes_unobserved_time']`.\n- **Frames with no tracked tongue, or velocity outliers**: excluded from the bin mean; a bin left with no valid frame becomes the explicit `'not visible'` class rather than being imputed.\n- **Malformed photostim entries** and **per-file failures**: a stop-before-start laser interval is swapped rather than silently producing an empty mask, and `_worker` catches any exception per file, reports it with a traceback, and lets the rest of the conversion finish.\n\nii.\n```python\n        classification = np.asarray(units['classification'][:]).astype(str)\n        good = np.where(classification == 'good')[0]\n        if len(good) == 0:\n            return {'identifier': ident, 'dropped': 'no good units'}\n```\n\n```python\n        spikes_per_trial = fr.sum(axis=(0, 2))\n        rec = spikes_per_trial > 0\n        ...\n        if ntr < 2:\n            return {'identifier': ident, 'dropped': 'fewer than 2 trials with ephys'}\n```\n\n```python\n        if off_rel < on_rel:                      # guard against corrupt entries\n            on_rel, off_rel = off_rel, on_rel\n```\n\n```python\n    cls = np.full(y_binned.shape, 3, dtype=np.int64)     # 3 = not visible\n```\n\n```python\ndef _worker(args):\n    path, show = args\n    try:\n        return convert_session(path, show_processing=show)\n    except Exception as e:  # pragma: no cover - defensive\n        import traceback\n        return {'identifier': os.path.basename(path), 'error': traceback.format_exc()}\n```\n\niii. CONVERSION_NOTES.md Step 5 Key Decision 6: \"**Unobserved time**: spikes exist only inside `[start_time, stop_time]` (= `obs_intervals`). 96.9 % of trials cover go−2.5 s, 84.4 % cover go+1.5 s (miss trials end early). The script instruments every stage and prints per-stage means. Per session: reading the ragged `spike_times` (0.40 s), binning the spikes (0.34 s), unit metadata + electrode/CCF lookup (0.09 s), tongue/output construction (0.08 s), trials and inputs (≈ 0 s) — so raw NWB I/O plus spike binning dominate, as expected. At whole-run level the two costs are the 174 per-session conversions (22.4 s wall clock across 24 worker processes; ≈ 0.9 s × 174 ≈ 160 s of CPU) and serialising the 11.89 GB pickle (18.7 s). Total 42 s, well inside the instructions' 15-minute budget.\n\nii.\n```python\n        t0 = time.time()\n        spike_lists = [np.asarray(units['spike_times'][int(i)]) for i in good]\n        timing['spike_read'] = time.time() - t0\n        t0 = time.time()\n        fr = bin_spikes(spike_lists, go[kidx])                    # (n_neurons, ntr, NBINS)\n        timing['binning'] = time.time() - t0\n```\n\n```python\n    tt_ = [i['timing'] for i in session_info]\n    for k in tt_[0]:\n        print('timing %-12s mean %.2f s/session' % (k, np.mean([t[k] for t in tt_])))\n    print('total elapsed %.1f s' % (time.time() - t_all))\n```\n\niii. CONVERSION_NOTES.md Step 6 \"Efficiency\" and Step 7 \"Run Time Estimates\" record the measured per-step costs and the speed-ups: \"`searchsorted` binning over all trial edges at once — 0.16 s/session (vs ~30 s for a naive Python loop)\"; \"`VectorIndex`-based electrode lookup — 0.09 s/session (vs ~10 s using `units['electrodes'][i]`)\"; \"16-way process parallelism — ~16×\". The estimate made from the 2-session sample (\"< 5 minutes\", scaled by ~1.3 for session size) was borne out by the 42 s full run reported in Step 9.\n\n## 10-b. What loops in the code could have been vectorized to improve efficiency?\n\ni. Several loops remain, in decreasing order of cost:\n\n- **Per-unit spike read**, `[np.asarray(units['spike_times'][int(i)]) for i in good]`: one ragged `VectorIndex` access (and therefore one HDF5 read) per unit, ~400 per session. All NWB times (spike times, event timestamps, camera timestamps) are on the same session-absolute clock, so no resampling or per-stream offset correction is required. Alignment is done by adding the fixed go-cue-relative edge grid to each trial's go-cue time (`go_start_times`, one per trial) and binning the raw spikes against those absolute edges. `metadata['temporal_alignment_event']` records the choice.\n\nii.\n```python\nOFF_START = -2.5          # s relative to go cue\nOFF_END = 1.5             # s relative to go cue\nNBINS = int(round((OFF_END - OFF_START) / BIN_SIZE))   # 80\nBIN_EDGES_REL = OFF_START + BIN_SIZE * np.arange(NBINS + 1)\nBIN_CENTERS_REL = BIN_EDGES_REL[:-1] + BIN_SIZE / 2\n```\n\n```python\n        go = np.asarray(be['go_start_times'].timestamps[:], dtype=float)\n```\n\n```python\n    edges = (go_times[:, None] + BIN_EDGES_REL[None, :]).ravel()\n    out = np.empty((len(spike_times_list), ntr, NBINS), dtype=np.float32)\n    for k, st in enumerate(spike_times_list):\n        idx = np.searchsorted(st, edges).reshape(ntr, NBINS + 1)\n        out[k] = np.diff(idx, axis=1)\n```\n\n```python\n            'temporal_alignment_event': 'auditory go cue onset (BehavioralEvents go_start_times)',\n            'off_start': OFF_START,\n            'off_end': OFF_END,\n```\n\niii. CONVERSION_NOTES.md Step 3: \"**Alignment**: everything aligned to the **go cue** (t = 0) in both papers; reference epochs sample [−1.85, −1.2] s, delay [−1.2, 0] s, response [0, 1.5] s.\" Step 4: \"spike/behaviour times minus `go_start_times` … ✓ same\" as the reference, which exported spike times already aligned to the go cue. What is the temporal resolution (time bin size) of the converted data? Is any temporal rebinning applied?\n\ni. 50 ms, giving 80 non-overlapping bins spanning −2.5 s to +1.5 s relative to the go cue, identical for every trial and every session. The grid is defined once at module level (81 relative edges, 80 relative centres) and reused everywhere, so the neural, input and output streams all share the same bins. There is no rebinning of an already-binned product: spikes are binned once directly from raw spike times, and the video (native dt = 3.4 ms) is averaged once into the same 50 ms grid. The bin width is exported as `metadata['time_bin_size'] = 50.0` (ms), with the bin centres also stored.\n\nii.\n```python\nBIN_SIZE = 0.05           # s, 50 ms bins (decoder task specification)\nOFF_START = -2.5          # s relative to go cue\nOFF_END = 1.5             # s relative to go cue\nNBINS = int(round((OFF_END - OFF_START) / BIN_SIZE))   # 80\nBIN_EDGES_REL = OFF_START + BIN_SIZE * np.arange(NBINS + 1)\nBIN_CENTERS_REL = BIN_EDGES_REL[:-1] + BIN_SIZE / 2\n```\n\n```python\n            'time_bin_size': BIN_SIZE * 1000.0,\n            'time_bin_size_units': 'ms',\n            ...\n            'bin_centers_re_go_cue_s': BIN_CENTERS_REL.tolist(),\n```\n\niii. CONVERSION_NOTES.md Step 3: the method paper \"binned spikes into firing rates with a bin width of 40 ms and a stride of 3.4 ms\", but \"Our task specifies **50 ms bins**, which we implement as non-overlapping 50 ms bins giving rates in Hz (80 bins over −2.5→+1.5 s)\". Step 4: \"Task specifies **50 ms bins** → non-overlapping 50 ms bins, rates in Hz (counts/0.05 s), 80 bins for −2.5→+1.5 s\", and Step 5 Key Decision 5: \"Bin *i* covers [−2.5 + 0.05 i, −2.45 + 0.05 i); the value assigned to input/output time series uses the **bin centre**.\" Step 10 Check 5 verifies the half-open-bin convention: \"`searchsorted` with `side='left'` makes bins half-open, so no spike is counted twice — verified by summing counts over bins and comparing with a direct count in [−2.5, 1.5) (equal).\" The verifier confirms `T: min 80, max 80` over the whole dataset.\n\n## 3-a. What variables in the raw data is `input` *Time from tone onset in seconds* derived from?\n\ni. From `BehavioralEvents/sample_start_times` (the onsets of the sample/tone epoch), `trials.start_time` (used to assign each sample event to a trial), and `go_start_times`. For each trial the tone taken is the **last** `sample_start` that belongs to that trial and occurs at or before its go cue, because an early lick replays the sample epoch and a trial can therefore carry several sample-start events.\n\nii.\n```python\ndef tone_onset_times(sample_starts, trial_starts, go_times):\n    \"\"\"Last sample(tone)-epoch start at or before the go cue, for each trial.\n\n    Early licking triggers a replay of the sample/delay epoch, so a trial can contain several\n    `sample_start_times`; the *last* one before the go cue is the tone the animal responded to.\n    \"\"\"\n    ntr = len(go_times)\n    out = np.full(ntr, np.nan)\n    if len(sample_starts):\n        tidx = np.searchsorted(trial_starts, sample_starts, side='right') - 1\n        ok = (tidx >= 0) & (tidx < ntr)\n        tidx, ev = tidx[ok], sample_starts[ok]\n        ok2 = ev <= go_times[tidx]\n        tidx, ev = tidx[ok2], ev[ok2]\n        order = np.argsort(ev, kind='stable')          # ascending -> last write wins\n        out[tidx[order]] = ev[order]\n    return out\n```\n\n```python\n        sample_starts = np.asarray(be['sample_start_times'].timestamps[:], dtype=float)\n        ...\n        tone = tone_onset_times(sample_starts, trial_start, go)[kidx]\n```\n\niii. CONVERSION_NOTES.md Step 2: \"`sample_*` and `delay_*` have **more** events than trials because early licking triggers a **replay** of the sample/delay epoch (confirmed: extra sample events occur only in `early` trials)\"; \"Last `sample_start` before the go cue is ~1.85–1.95 s before the go cue (tone onset); this matches the paper's sample epoch start at −1.85 s and 1.2 s delay.\" Step 4: \"Early-lick trials trigger epoch *replays*, so the **last** sample start before the go cue is the tone the animal actually used.\" Step 5 mapping: \"median = 1.85 s before the go cue in every session; using the **last** sample start handles early-lick replays.\" The verifier reports the median tone onset at exactly −1.850 s re go cue across all 173 sessions.\n\n## 3-b. What processing is involved in computing `input` *Time from tone onset in seconds*?\n\ni. The tone time is expressed relative to the trial's go cue (`tone_rel_go = tone − go`, typically ≈ −1.85 s), and each bin's value is its go-cue-relative centre minus that offset, i.e. seconds elapsed since tone onset at that bin centre. The result is a continuous, time-varying `float32` row of length 80, stored as row 0 of the per-trial `(2, 80)` input array. Values run from ≈ −0.65 s (bin before the tone on a normal trial) upward; the full converted range is [−1.525, 5.936] s, with the large values coming from early-lick replay trials where the final tone is close to the go cue but earlier bins reach back before an earlier replay.\n\nii.\n```python\n        tone = tone_onset_times(sample_starts, trial_start, go)[kidx]\n        tone_rel_go = tone - go[kidx]                             # negative, ~ -1.85 s\n        # time since tone onset at each bin centre (s)\n        time_from_tone = (BIN_CENTERS_REL[None, :] - tone_rel_go[:, None]).astype(np.float32)\n```\n\n```python\n        input_trials = [np.stack([time_from_tone[i], photostim[i]]).astype(np.float32)\n                        for i in range(ntr)]\n```\n\niii. CONVERSION_NOTES.md Step 5 mapping table: \"last `sample_start_times` ≤ go cue, per trial → `input[0]` = `time_from_tone_onset_s`; bin-center time − tone-onset time (seconds), continuous, time-varying (80 values)\". Step 5 Key Decision 5 fixes the bin-centre convention for input/output time series. Planned sanity check: \"`input[0]` (time from tone onset) ≈ −0.65 … 3.35 s with median tone onset at −1.85 s re go cue\"; Step 9 reports the achieved range [−1.53, 11.9] s (the max in the pickle summary is 5.936 s; the verifier reports 11.9 s) and explains it as \"long values come from early-lick replay trials\". Step 10 Check 2 verified the full 80-bin time-from-tone vector against independently recomputed values for 4 random trials in each of 4 sessions.\n\n## 3-c. How is the `input` *Time from tone onset in seconds* aligned with the neural data?\n\ni. It is constructed *on* the neural bin grid: the same module-level `BIN_CENTERS_REL` array that defines the 80 spike bins is what is shifted by the tone-to-go-cue gap. Bin *k* of the input therefore refers to exactly the interval whose spikes are in bin *k* of `neural`, by construction — no interpolation or index matching is needed.\n\nii.\n```python\nBIN_EDGES_REL = OFF_START + BIN_SIZE * np.arange(NBINS + 1)\nBIN_CENTERS_REL = BIN_EDGES_REL[:-1] + BIN_SIZE / 2\n```\n\n```python\n    edges = (go_times[:, None] + BIN_EDGES_REL[None, :]).ravel()   # neural bins\n```\n\n```python\n        time_from_tone = (BIN_CENTERS_REL[None, :] - tone_rel_go[:, None]).astype(np.float32)\n```\n\niii. CONVERSION_NOTES.md Step 5 mapping table: \"`BehavioralEvents['photostim_start_times' / 'photostim_stop_times'].timestamps` → `input[1]` = `photostim_on` … `stimulation[:,2:] -= gocue_time` (reference stores on/off times re go cue) … cross-checked against the `trials.photostim_onset/power/duration` columns.\" The AI verified the stimulation parameters against the papers (Step 4: \"18,588/94,990 trials (19.6 %) at 5.5 mW, always 0.5 s; onset −1.2 s or −0.5 s re go cue\" vs \"~25 % randomly interleaved trials, 5 mW/hemisphere, last 0.5 s of delay\"; \"Stim always **ends before the go cue** ✓ (max stim end = go − 0.499 s)\"). Each laser event is assigned to the trial whose `start_time` last precedes it; the on/off times are converted to go-cue-relative seconds; a bin is set to 1 if the stimulation interval **overlaps** the bin interval (`bin_start < off` and `bin_end > on`), 0 otherwise. Trials with no laser event stay all-zero. A defensive swap handles any entry where the stop time precedes the start time. Stored as `float32` row 1 of the `(2, 80)` input array.\n\nii.\n```python\ndef photostim_binary(stim_on, stim_off, trial_starts, go_times):\n    \"\"\"(n_trials, NBINS) binary array: is photostimulation on during this bin?\"\"\"\n    ntr = len(go_times)\n    ps = np.zeros((ntr, NBINS), dtype=np.float32)\n    if len(stim_on) == 0:\n        return ps\n    tidx = np.searchsorted(trial_starts, stim_on, side='right') - 1\n    for i, on, off in zip(tidx, stim_on, stim_off):\n        if i < 0 or i >= ntr:\n            continue\n        on_rel, off_rel = on - go_times[i], off - go_times[i]\n        if off_rel < on_rel:                      # guard against corrupt entries\n            on_rel, off_rel = off_rel, on_rel\n        # a bin is 'on' if the stimulation interval overlaps the bin\n        overlap = (BIN_EDGES_REL[:-1] < off_rel) & (BIN_EDGES_REL[1:] > on_rel)\n        ps[i, overlap] = 1.0\n    return ps\n```\n\niii. CONVERSION_NOTES.md Step 5 mapping table: \"1 if the 50 ms bin overlaps [stim_on, stim_off] (times re go cue), else 0; binary time-varying\". The instructions require \"Whether **photostimulation** is on at every time point (discrete, time-varying)\" and \"If an input is a time such as onset of some stimulus, represent it as a binary time series\", which the AI cites in Step 5 Key Decision 9. Step 3 confirms the cameras run at 300 Hz per the data paper.\n\n## 8-b. What processing is involved in computing `output` *Tongue y-position*?\n\ni. Four steps:\n1. **Visibility mask** — frames with `likelihood > 0.5` count as visible (the tracker still emits a position when the tongue is retracted).\n2. **Outlier rejection** — among the visible frames, the inter-frame velocity `dy/dt` is computed and frames following a jump larger than 5 σ are invalidated, following the method paper's 5-sigma velocity outlier rule.\n3. **Binning** — for each trial, the valid frames inside `[go − 2.5, go + 1.5)` are averaged (via `np.bincount` sum/count) into the same 80 × 50 ms bins; a bin with no valid frame is left `NaN`.\n4. **Discretisation** — per session, the 40th and 60th percentiles of *all finite binned values* are taken and each bin is assigned class 0/1/2; `NaN` bins become class 3, \"not visible\".\n\nNo mean-imputation is done for occluded frames (the method paper imputes the mean), because the task requires an explicit \"not visible\" category.\n\nii.\n```python\nTONGUE_LIK_THRESH = 0.5   # DeepLabCut likelihood above which the tongue is 'visible'\nVELOCITY_SIGMA = 5.0      # 5-sigma velocity outlier rejection (method paper)\n```\n\n```python\ndef bin_tongue(ts, y, lik, go_times):\n    \"\"\"Mean visible tongue y-position per 50 ms bin, NaN where the tongue is not visible.\"\"\"\n    ntr = len(go_times)\n    visible = lik > TONGUE_LIK_THRESH\n    valid = visible.copy()\n    if visible.sum() > 10:\n        iv = np.where(visible)[0]\n        dy = np.diff(y[iv]) / np.maximum(np.diff(ts[iv]), 1e-6)\n        s = np.std(dy)\n        if s > 0:\n            bad = np.abs(dy) > VELOCITY_SIGMA * s\n            # a large jump invalidates the frame after the jump\n            valid[iv[1:][bad]] = False\n    res = np.full((ntr, NBINS), np.nan, dtype=np.float32)\n    t0 = go_times + OFF_START\n    lo = np.searchsorted(ts, t0)\n    hi = np.searchsorted(ts, go_times + OFF_END)\n    for i in range(ntr):\n        a, b = lo[i], hi[i]\n        if b <= a:\n            continue\n        tsel = ts[a:b]\n        vsel = valid[a:b]\n        if not vsel.any():\n            continue\n        bi = np.floor((tsel[vsel] - t0[i]) / BIN_SIZE).astype(int)\n        np.clip(bi, 0, NBINS - 1, out=bi)\n        cnt = np.bincount(bi, minlength=NBINS)\n        sm = np.bincount(bi, weights=y[a:b][vsel], minlength=NBINS)\n        nz = cnt > 0\n        res[i, nz] = (sm[nz] / cnt[nz]).astype(np.float32)\n    return res\n```\n\niii. CONVERSION_NOTES.md Step 3: \"**Video markers**: DeepLabCut side-view tongue/jaw/nose; outliers detected by 5-sigma velocity threshold and imputed from nearby frames; when the tongue is occluded (in the mouth) the method paper sets tongue position to its mean value. Our decoder task instead requires an explicit 'not visible' class (class 3), so occlusion is represented as its own category (detected via DLC likelihood).\" Step 5 Key Decision 7: \"**Tongue visibility threshold**: `likelihood > 0.5`. The likelihood distribution is strongly bimodal (89 % < 0.1, 10 % > 0.9) so the exact threshold is immaterial.\" Step 5 Key Decision 8: \"**Percentiles computed per session** over the *binned, visible* tongue-y values of the exported trials, so the resulting class frequencies are exactly 40 / 20 / 40 % of visible bins in each session.\" (Note: the Step 5 mapping table says \"median y of frames in that bin\" while the code, its docstring, Step 6 and the README all say the bin **mean**; the code computes the mean.) Step 10 Check 2 recomputed the complete tongue class matrix from raw DLC data for 4 sessions with independent code: \"✓ agreement 1.0000\".\n\n## 8-c. How is `output` *Tongue y-position* thresholded into categories?\n\ni. Per session, the 40th and 60th percentiles of the finite (visible) binned y-values are computed and used as the two class edges: `y < p40 → 0`, `p40 ≤ y ≤ p60 → 1`, `y > p60 → 2`; `NaN` (no visible frame in the bin) → `3`. The percentiles and the visible fraction are recorded per session in `session_info` (`tongue_p40`, `tongue_p60`, `frac_bins_tongue_visible`). Because the percentiles are taken over exactly the quantity being discretised, the visible bins split exactly 40/20/40 within each session; over the whole dataset the classes come out 0.101 / 0.050 / 0.101 / 0.749.\n\nii.\n```python\ndef discretize_tongue(y_binned):\n    \"\"\"Per-session discretisation of tongue y into 4 classes (task specification).\"\"\"\n    vis = np.isfinite(y_binned)\n    cls = np.full(y_binned.shape, 3, dtype=np.int64)     # 3 = not visible\n    if vis.sum() > 0:\n        p40, p60 = np.percentile(y_binned[vis], [40, 60])\n        v = y_binned[vis]\n        c = np.where(v < p40, 0, np.where(v <= p60, 1, 2))\n        cls[vis] = c\n    else:\n        p40 = p60 = np.nan\n    return cls, float(p40), float(p60)\n```\n\n```python\nOUTPUT_VALUES = [\n    ...\n    ['<40th pct', '40-60th pct', '>60th pct', 'not visible'],\n]\n```\n\niii. Do NOT look outside this project directory.\n\n**Goal**: Understand how the original authors loaded and processed their data.\n\n**Actions**:\n# Decisions\n\n## 1-a. How are **all the data** for all subjects, sessions, and trials loaded in?\n\ni. The dataset is distributed as one NWB file per session under `data/sub-<subject_id>/`. All sessions are found with a single glob over that layout, and each file is opened with `pynwb` and processed once. Subjects, trials, and units are then read from within each file (`nwb.subject`, `nwb.trials`, `nwb.units`, `nwb.acquisition`).\n\nii. Finding all data:\n```python\nfiles = sorted(glob.glob(os.path.join(DATA_DIR, 'sub-*', '*.nwb')))\n...\nfor i, path in enumerate(files, 1):\n    res = process_session(path)\n```\n\nLoading one session:\n```python\nwith NWBHDF5IO(path, mode='r', load_namespaces=True) as io:\n    nwb = io.read()\n    units = nwb.units\n    trials = nwb.trials.to_dataframe()\n    bev = nwb.acquisition['BehavioralEvents'].time_series\n```\n\niii. NWB is the published format for this dataset and `pynwb` is its standard reader. Since there is one file per session, the directory listing is the complete set of sessions and a glob is sufficient; sorting it makes the session order deterministic. The resulting counts (174 files, 28 subjects) match `assetsSummary` in `data/dandiset.yaml`.\n\n## 1-b. How are the data split into subjects?\n\ni. Each NWB file records its animal in `nwb.subject.subject_id`, a numeric string such as `'440956'`. That value is read for every session and carried through to assembly, where `subjects` is the sorted set of unique ids and `subject_idx` gives each session's index into that list.\n\nii. Per session:\n```python\nreturn {\n    'session_id': nwb.identifier,\n    'subject': nwb.subject.subject_id,\n    ...\n```\n\nAt assembly:\n```python\nsubjects = sorted({r['subject'] for r in results})\nsub_ix = {s: i for i, s in enumerate(subjects)}\n...\n'subjects': subjects,\n'subject_idx': np.array([sub_ix[r['subject']] for r in results], np.int32),\n```\n\niii. `subject_id` is the canonical animal identifier in the file, and the containing folder name (`sub-440956`) is derived from it, so no separate grouping step is needed. This gives 28 subjects with 3-10 sessions each, matching the dandiset. The numeric id differs from the mouse name used in the papers — `nwb.identifier` is e.g. `SC015_20190207_120657_s1`, so subject `440956` is mouse `SC015` — but the numeric id is what the NWB subject field provides, so it is used directly.\n\n## 1-c. How are the data split into sessions?\n\ni. One NWB file is one session, so no grouping or splitting is needed. Each session is identified by `nwb.identifier` (e.g. `SC015_20190207_120657_s1`, encoding mouse, date, time and session number), recorded per session and also listed in `metadata['session_info']`. Session order in the output follows the sorted file list.\n\nii.\n```python\nfiles = sorted(glob.glob(os.path.join(DATA_DIR, 'sub-*', '*.nwb')))\n```\n\n```python\n'session_id': nwb.identifier,\n```\n\n```python\n'session_info': [\n    {'session_id': r['session_id'], 'subject': r['subject'],\n     'n_trials': r['n_trials'], 'n_units': r['n_units']}\n    for r in results\n],\n```\n\niii. The dandiset already stores one session per file, so the file boundary is the session boundary and nothing has to be inferred. Because the filename embeds the acquisition timestamp (`sub-440956_ses-20190207T120657_...`), sorting the paths puts sessions in chronological order within each subject. 173 of the 174 files reach the output; the one exception is dropped for having no quality-controlled units (see 2-c).\n\n## 1-d. Are the data correctly split into trials?\n\ni. Trials come from the NWB trials table (`nwb.trials`), one row per behavioural trial, with exactly one go-cue event per row. The row count is checked against the number of go-cue events.\n\nii.\n```python\ntrials = nwb.trials.to_dataframe()\ngo = np.asarray(bev['go_start_times'].timestamps)\nassert len(go) == len(trials), f'{len(go)} go cues vs {len(trials)} trials'\n```\n\niii. Trials are clearly defined by the trials table, so it is used directly rather than re-deriving boundaries from the event streams. `go_start_times` has exactly one event per trial in all 174 sessions, which makes the mapping unambiguous. This is not true of the other trial-phase events: `sample_start_times` and `delay_start_times` can have several entries per trial, because a lick during the sample or delay replays that epoch.\n\n## 1-e. How are trials filtered based on quality controls?\n\ni. Trials are filtered only for absence of spike data, in two cases. First, trials outside `units/obs_intervals`: in 8 sessions the ephys recording starts after the behaviour, leaving up to 376 leading trials with no spikes. Second, `free_water` trials, which have no spikes anywhere in the window even though `obs_intervals` covers them. A session is dropped entirely if fewer than 2 trials survive. No behavioural quality filter is applied.\n\nii.\n```python\n# filter behavioral trials with no spike data\noi_off = np.asarray(units['obs_intervals'].data)\noi_start = np.concatenate([[0], oi_off[:-1]])\nobs = np.asarray(units['obs_intervals'].target.data)[oi_start[good[0]]:oi_off[good[0]]]\nkeep = np.isin(np.round(trials['start_time'].values, 4), np.round(obs[:, 0], 4))\nassert keep.sum() == len(obs), f'{keep.sum()} matched vs {len(obs)} observed'\n\n# filter no water trials\nkeep &= trials['free_water'].values == 0\nif keep.sum() < 2:\n    return None\ntrials = trials[keep]\ngo = go[keep]\n```\n\niii. `obs_intervals` is the file's own record of which trials were observed, and its start times match `trials.start_time`, which makes the mapping exact. The `free_water` exclusion was found empirically — those trials are covered by `obs_intervals` yet contain no spikes at all — and accounts for 2,449 of the 2,451 all-zero trials remaining after the `obs_intervals` filter.\n\nEarly-lick and no-response (`ignore`) trials are deliberately kept, even though the data paper states \"Early lick trials and no response trials were excluded for analysis\", because both are required decoder outputs here. The 2-trial minimum is the target format's requirement.\n\nTogether these remove 3,510 of the 94,370 trials in the retained sessions (3.7%), leaving 90,860.\n\n## 2-a. What variables in the raw data is the final `neural` data derived from?\n\ni. Neural data is derived from `units/spike_times`, the sorted spike times of each unit in session-absolute seconds. Only units with `classification == 'good'` contribute (see 2-c). The go-cue times (`BehavioralEvents/go_start_times`) are the other input, used to place the bin edges.\n\nii.\n```python\noffs = np.asarray(units['spike_times'].data)\nallst = np.asarray(units['spike_times'].target.data)\nstarts = np.concatenate([[0], offs[:-1]])\n\nedges = (go[:, None] + REL_EDGES[None, :]).ravel()\nrates = np.empty((good.size, n_trials, N_BINS), np.float32)\nfor r, u in enumerate(good):\n    s = allst[starts[u]:offs[u]]\n```\n\niii. `spike_times` is the only neural representation in the file, so firing rates are computed from it directly.\n\n## 2-b. How is the `neural` data processed?\n\ni. Spike times are converted to per-bin firing rates in Hz. For each good unit, the bin edges for every trial are built as one flat array of absolute times, `np.searchsorted` gives the running spike count at each edge, and differencing adjacent counts gives the spike count per bin. Counts are divided by the bin width to give Hz. No smoothing, normalisation, or baseline subtraction is applied.\n\nii.\n```python\nedges = (go[:, None] + REL_EDGES[None, :]).ravel()\nrates = np.empty((good.size, n_trials, N_BINS), np.float32)\nfor r, u in enumerate(good):\n    s = allst[starts[u]:offs[u]]\n    # running spike total at each edge; differencing gives the count per bin\n    pos = np.searchsorted(s, edges).reshape(n_trials, N_BINS + 1)\n    rates[r] = np.diff(pos, axis=1)\nrates /= BIN                                  # counts -> Hz\n```\n\niii. Firing rate is computed from the binned spike count over the 50 ms window defined in the instructions. This also matches the reference code, which calls `sliding_histogram(..., rate=True)` and returns `binSpikes / bin_width`.\n\n## 2-c. How is the `neural` data filtered based on quality controls?\n\ni. Only units with `units/classification == 'good'` are kept. No thresholds are applied to any individual quality metric. A session with no such units is dropped entirely. This retains 69,453 of 272,227 units (25.5%), a median of 390 per session.\n\nii.\n```python\n# ---- units: QC classifier verdict ----------------------------------\ncls = _text(units['classification'])\ngood = np.flatnonzero(cls == 'good')\nif good.size == 0:\n    return None\n```\n\niii. `classification` is the verdict of the spike-sorting quality-control classifier described in `ChenLiuEtAl2023_SpikeSortingQC.pdf`.\n\n`units/unit_quality` ('good' / 'multi') is deliberately not used: it is an older label that disagrees on 12.2% of the classifier-good units and is far more permissive.\n\nThe one dropped session (`sub-440958_ses-20190216T162508`) has `classification` and `anno_name` set to NaN for all 1,852 units, i.e. it was never quality-controlled. Excluding it gives 173 sessions and 69,453 good units, against the white paper's 173 sessions and 69,943 units.\n\n## 2-d. How is the per-trial `neural` data aligned to the event described in the `instructions`?\n\ni. Spike times and event times are already on the same session-absolute clock, so no alignment step is needed. The bin edges relative to the go cue are added to each trial's go-cue time to give the absolute time window for that trial, and the spikes are binned against those edges directly.\n\nii.\n```python\ngo = np.asarray(bev['go_start_times'].timestamps)\n```\n\n```python\nedges = (go[:, None] + REL_EDGES[None, :]).ravel()\nrates = np.empty((good.size, n_trials, N_BINS), np.float32)\nfor r, u in enumerate(good):\n    s = allst[starts[u]:offs[u]]\n    pos = np.searchsorted(s, edges).reshape(n_trials, N_BINS + 1)\n    rates[r] = np.diff(pos, axis=1)\n```\n\niii. Everything in the NWB file is timestamped on one global clock, so aligning to the go cue only requires looking up each trial's go-cue time and taking the window around it. There is no resampling or interpolation, and no per-stream offset to correct.\n\n## 2-e. How is the `neural` data temporally binned/resampled?\n\ni. Spike times are binned into 80 non-overlapping 50 ms bins spanning -2.5 s to +1.5 s relative to the go cue. The bin grid is defined once, as 81 edges relative to the go cue, and reused for every trial and session, so every trial has the same 80 timepoints.\n\nii.\n```python\n# trial window relative to the go cue, and bin width, in seconds\nT_START, T_STOP = -2.5, 1.5\nBIN = 0.05\nN_BINS = int(round((T_STOP - T_START) / BIN))             \n\nREL_EDGES = T_START + BIN * np.arange(N_BINS + 1)         \nCENTERS = REL_EDGES[:-1] + BIN / 2                        \n```\n\n```python\nedges = (go[:, None] + REL_EDGES[None, :]).ravel()\n```\n\niii. The window and the 50 ms bin width are set by the instructions. Defining the grid once as offsets from the go cue gives a constant 80 timepoints per trial, which the target format requires.\n\n## 3-a. What variables in the raw data is `input` *time_from_tone_onset* derived from?\n\ni. From `sample_start_times`, the tone onsets of the session, together with the go cue of each trial. The tone taken for a trial is the **last one** before its go cue.\n\nii. The tone of each trial:\n```python\nsample = np.asarray(bev['sample_start_times'].timestamps)\ntone = sample[np.searchsorted(sample, go, side='left') - 1]\n```\n\niii. An early lick replays the sample epoch, so a trial can carry more than one tone; the last one before the go cue is the one the animal actually used.\n\n## 3-b. What processing is involved in computing `input` *time_from_tone_onset*?\n\ni. The bins sit around the go cue, so the value of a bin is its center plus the gap between the tone and the go cue.\n\nii. The bin center, and the shift that turns them into time from the tone:\n```python\nCENTERS = REL_EDGES[:-1] + BIN / 2                        \n```\n```python\n# bins sit around the go cue, values are seconds since the tone\ntime_from_tone = CENTERS[None, :] + (go - tone)[:, None]\n```\n\niii. No additional processing needed other than find the tone onset time.\n\n## 3-c. How is `input` *time_from_tone_onset* aligned with the neural data?\n\ni. It is how the neural binnning grid is defined.\n\nii. The grid, defined once as offsets from the go cue, and laid on each trial's go cue to bin the spikes:\n```python\nT_START, T_STOP = -2.5, 1.5\nBIN = 0.05\nN_BINS = int(round((T_STOP - T_START) / BIN))             \n\nREL_EDGES = T_START + BIN * np.arange(N_BINS + 1)         \nCENTERS = REL_EDGES[:-1] + BIN / 2                        \n```\n```python\nedges = (go[:, None] + REL_EDGES[None, :]).ravel()\n```\n\niii. N/A\n\n## 4-a. What variables in the raw data is `input` *photostim* derived from?\n\ni. From `photostim_onset` and `photostim_duration` in the trials table, with `start_time` and the go cue used to place them on the trial's time axis.\n\nii. The onset and offset of the stimulation, relative to the go cue:\n```python\non_s = trials['photostim_onset'].values\nhas = on_s != 'N/A'\nstim_on[has] = trials['start_time'].values[has] + on_s[has].astype(float) - go[has]\nstim_off[has] = stim_on[has] + trials['photostim_duration'].values[has].astype(float)\n```\n\niii. The onsets are stored as strings measured from trial start, with `'N/A'` on the trials that were not stimulated, so they have to be converted and re-expressed against the go cue the bins are aligned on.\n\n## 4-b. What processing is involved in computing `input` *photostim*?\n\ni. A bin is 1 where its center falls between the onset and the offset of the stimulation and 0 elsewhere, so the input is a binary time series rather than a per trial flag.\n\nii. The bins the light is on for:\n```python\n# NaN compares False, so non-stim trials stay 0\nphotostim = ((CENTERS[None, :] >= stim_on[:, None])\n             & (CENTERS[None, :] < stim_off[:, None]))\n```\n\niii. A trial without stimulation keeps NaN bounds, and NaN compares false, so all of its bins come out 0 without a separate branch.\n\n#!/usr/bin/env python3\n\"\"\"Convert the Brain-wide Activity Map dataset (DANDI 000363) to the decoder format.\n\n    python -u convert_data.py <outpicklefile> [--full | --sample] [--datadir DIR]\n\"\"\"\n\nimport argparse\nimport glob\nimport os\nimport pickle\nimport re\nimport sys\nimport time\n\nimport numpy as np\nfrom pynwb import NWBHDF5IO\n\n_chen2024_seed = 'x5cidj2hy87s'\nnp.random.seed(sum(ord(c) for c in _chen2024_seed) % 2**31)\n\nHERE = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))\n# Default only, for running this by hand from manual/chen2024/. The oracle arm runs\n# the script from /solution while the dataset is mounted read-only at /app/data, so\n# solve.sh overrides this with --datadir.\nDATA_DIR = os.path.join(HERE, 'data')\n\n# trial window relative to the go cue, and bin width, in seconds\nT_START, T_STOP = -2.5, 1.5\nBIN = 0.05\nN_BINS = int(round((T_STOP - T_START) / BIN))             # 80\n\nREL_EDGES = T_START + BIN * np.arange(N_BINS + 1)         # 81 edges, re go cue\nCENTERS = REL_EDGES[:-1] + BIN / 2                        # 80 bin centres\n\nOUTCOME_CODE = {'ignore': 0, 'miss': 1, 'hit': 2}\nEARLY_CODE = {'no early': 0, 'early': 1}\nSIDE_CODE = {'left': 0, 'right': 1}\nCHOICE_NO_LICK = 2               # no lick in the response window\nTONGUE_HIDDEN = 3                # no visible tongue frame in the bin\n\nTONGUE_CONF = 0.5                # tracking likelihood for the tongue to count as visible\nTONGUE_PCT = (40, 60)            # per-session percentiles -> 3 visible classes\n\nINPUT_NAMES = ['time_from_tone_onset', 'photostim']\nOUTPUT_NAMES = ['choice', 'outcome', 'early_lick', 'tongue_y_position']\n\n# output_values[i][code] names each value of output i\nOUTPUT_VALUES = [\n    ['left', 'right', 'no lick'],\n    ['ignore', 'miss', 'hit'],\n    ['no', 'yes'],\n    ['below 40th pct', '40th to 60th pct', 'above 60th pct', 'not visible'],\n]\n\n\ndef region_label(anno):\n    \"\"\"'Orbital area, lateral part, layer 5' -> 'orbital area'.\"\"\"\n    return re.split(r'[,./]', anno)[0].strip().lower()\n\n\ndef _text(col):\n    \"\"\"Read a text column; non-str entries (unlabelled sessions) become ''.\"\"\"\n    return np.array([x if isinstance(x, str) else '' for x in col[:]])\n\n\ndef _bin_mean(idx, y, n):\n    \"\"\"Mean of y per bin given a per-sample bin index. NaN where a bin is empty.\"\"\"\n    ok = ~np.isnan(y)\n    tot = np.bincount(idx[ok], weights=y[ok], minlength=n)\n    cnt = np.bincount(idx[ok], minlength=n)\n    with np.errstate(invalid='ignore'):\n        return np.where(cnt > 0, tot / np.maximum(cnt, 1), np.nan)\n\n\ndef tongue_output(nwb, go):\n    \"\"\"Discretise tongue y into (n_trials, N_BINS) classes.\"\"\"\n    ts = nwb.acquisition['BehavioralTimeSeries'].time_series['Camera0_side_TongueTracking']\n    t_cam = np.asarray(ts.timestamps)\n    data = ts.data[:]                        # (n_frames, 3) = x, y, likelihood\n    y = data[:, 1].copy()\n    y[data[:, 2] < TONGUE_CONF] = np.nan     # keep only visible frames\n\n    # bin the whole session on one grid, then take percentiles of the bin means\n    gidx = np.floor((t_cam - t_cam[0]) / BIN).astype(np.int64)\n    edges = np.nanpercentile(_bin_mean(gidx, y, int(gidx[-1]) + 1), TONGUE_PCT)\n\n    # per trial, bin the same way and digitise against those edges\n    cls = np.full((len(go), N_BINS), TONGUE_HIDDEN, np.int8)\n    lo = np.searchsorted(t_cam, go + T_START, 'left')\n    hi = np.searchsorted(t_cam, go + T_STOP, 'left')\n    for i in range(len(go)):\n        b = np.floor((t_cam[lo[i]:hi[i]] - (go[i] + T_START)) / BIN).astype(np.int64)\n        np.clip(b, 0, N_BINS - 1, out=b)\n        m = _bin_mean(b, y[lo[i]:hi[i]], N_BINS)\n        ok = ~np.isnan(m)\n        cls[i, ok] = np.digitize(m[ok], edges)\n    return cls\n\n\ndef process_session(path):\n    \"\"\"Convert one NWB file. Returns a dict, or None if the session is dropped.\"\"\"\n    with NWBHDF5IO(path, mode='r', load_namespaces=True) as io:\n        nwb = io.read()\n        units = nwb.units\n        trials = nwb.trials.to_dataframe()\n        bev = nwb.acquisition['BehavioralEvents'].time_series\n\n        # ---- units: QC classifier verdict ----------------------------------\n        cls = _text(units['classification'])\n        good = np.flatnonzero(cls == 'good')\n        if good.size == 0:\n            return None\n        regions = [region_label(a) for a in _text(units['anno_name'])[good]]\n\n        # all NWB times are session-absolute seconds\n        go = np.asarray(bev['go_start_times'].timestamps)\n        assert len(go) == len(trials), f'{len(go)} go cues vs {len(trials)} trials'\n\n        # ---- trials filtering ----\n        # spike data\n        # obs_intervals gives one [start, stop] per observed trial, which in some\n        # sessions is fewer than the behavioural trials. \n        # a behavioural trial is observed if its start time is one of the interval starts\n        obs = np.asarray(units['obs_intervals'][good[0]])        \n        keep = np.isin(trials['start_time'].values, obs[:, 0])\n        assert keep.sum() == len(obs), f'{keep.sum()} matched vs {len(obs)} observed'\n\n        # filter no water trials\n        keep &= trials['free_water'].values == 0\n        \n        # a sessioon has to have at least 2 trials according to the instruction\n        if keep.sum() < 2:\n            return None\n        \n        trials = trials[keep]\n        go = go[keep]\n        n_trials = len(go)\n\n        # last tone onset before the go cue; ---------------- trials\n        t0 = time.time()\n        tr = nwb.trials\n        trial_start = np.asarray(tr['start_time'][:], dtype=float)\n        trial_stop = np.asarray(tr['stop_time'][:], dtype=float)\n        outcome = np.asarray(tr['outcome'][:]).astype(str)\n        instruction = np.asarray(tr['trial_instruction'][:]).astype(str)\n        early = np.asarray(tr['early_lick'][:]).astype(str)\n        auto_water = np.asarray(tr['auto_water'][:]).astype(int)\n        free_water = np.asarray(tr['free_water'][:]).astype(int)\n        stim_flag_tbl = np.asarray(tr['photostim_power'][:]).astype(str) != 'N/A'\n\n        be = nwb.acquisition['BehavioralEvents'].time_series\n        go = np.asarray(be['go_start_times'].timestamps[:], dtype=float)\n        sample_starts = np.asarray(be['sample_start_times'].timestamps[:], dtype=float)\n        stim_on = np.asarray(be['photostim_start_times'].timestamps[:], dtype=float)\n        stim_off = np.asarray(be['photostim_stop_times'].timestamps[:], dtype=float)\n        assert len(go) == len(trial_start), 'go cue count != trial count in %s' % ident\n        timing['trials'] = time.time() - t0\n\n        # trial curation: drop auto-water / free-water trials (reference get_regular_trial_mask);\n        # early-lick, ignore/miss and photostim trials are KEPT because they are decoder outputs\n        # / inputs in this task.\n        keep = (auto_water == 0) & (free_water == 0)\n        n_dropped_water = int((~keep).sum())\n        kidx = np.where(keep)[0]\n        ntr = len(kidx)\n        if ntr < 2:\n            return {'identifier': ident, 'dropped': 'fewer than 2 usable trials'}\n\n        # ---------------- neural: spikes -> firing rates aligned to the go cue\n        t0 = time.time()\n        spike_lists = [np.asarray(units['spike_times'][int(i)]) for i in good]\n        timing['spike_read'] = time.time() - t0\n        t0 = time.time()\n        fr = bin_spikes(spike_lists, go[kidx])                    # (n_neurons, ntr, NBINS)\n        timing['binning'] = time.time() - t0\n\n        # --- exclude trials with no ephys at all (acquisition gaps).\n        # In some sessions the probes stop before the behaviour does, or single trials are\n        # missing from the ephys stream; such trials contain zero spikes across *every* good\n        # unit in the whole analysis window.  They carry no neural information and would be\n        # pure noise for the decoder, so they are treated as invalid data periods and removed.\n        spikes_per_trial = fr.sum(axis=(0, 2))\n        rec = spikes_per_trial > 0\n        n_dropped_norec = int((~rec).sum())\n        if n_dropped_norec:\n            fr = fr[:, rec, :]\n            kidx = kidx[rec]\n            ntr = int(rec.sum())\n        if ntr < 2:\n            return {'identifier': ident, 'dropped': 'fewer than 2 trials with ephys'}\n\n        # ---------------- inputs\n        t0 = time.time()\n        tone = tone_onset_times(sample_starts, trial_start, go)[kidx]\n        tone_rel_go = tone - go[kidx]                             # negative, ~ -1.85 s\n        # time since tone onset at each bin centre (s)\n        time_from_tone = (BIN_CENTERS_REL[None, :] - tone_rel_go[:, None]).astype(np.float32)\n        ps_all = photostim_binary(stim_on, stim_off, trial_start, go)\n        photostim = ps_all[kidx]\n        timing['inputs'] = time.time() - t0\n\n        # ---------------- outputs\n        t0 = time.time()\n        out_k = outcome[kidx]\n        instr_k = instruction[kidx]\n        # choice: hit -> instructed side, miss -> opposite side, ignore -> no lick\n        choice = np.where(out_k == 'ignore', 2,\n                          np.where(out_k == 'hit',\n                                   np.where(instr_k == 'left', 0, 1),\n                                   np.where(instr_k == 'left', 1, 0))).astype(np.int64)\n        outcome_code = np.where(out_k == 'ignore', 0, np.where(out_k == 'miss', 1, 2)).astype(np.int64)\n        early_code = (early[kidx] == 'early').astype(np.int64)\n# Dataset Conversion Notes\n\n## Overview\n- **Dataset**: Brain-wide neural activity 0.04` s (40 ms sliding window), `stride = 0.0034` s (matches video frame period), `begin_time = -3.0`, `end_time = 3.0`, `qc_mode = 'classifier'`.\n- Firing rates are **spike counts / bin_width** (Hz), computed with a *sliding* window; for our task we are instructed to use 50-ms bins, so we will use non-overlapping 50-ms bins (stride = width = 50 ms), which is the natural analogue.\n- Epochs used in the paper (relative to go cue): sample `[-1.85, -1.2]` s, delay `[-1.2, 0]` s, response `[0, 1.5]` s. So the trial structure is ~1.3 s sample + 1.2 s delay; our window of -2.5 to +1.5 s around the go cue covers pre-sample, sample, delay and response.\n- Neuron QC in the reference is performed with an **external classifier-based good-unit list** (`goodunits/*.mat`) not shipped with the NWB data. The NWB `units` table (DANDI 000363) contains per-unit QC metrics (`unit_amp`, `presence_ratio`, `amplitude_cutoff`, `isi_violation`, `drift_metric`, `unit_quality`...) and typically a `unit_quality`/`quality` field; we will reproduce the QC using the criteria in the Chen/Liu et al. 2023 spike-sorting QC white paper (to be read in Step 3) applied to those metrics.\n- Units without CCF histology annotation are dropped in the reference (`unit_comb = set(ephys unit ids) & set(histology unit ids)`).\n- Hemisphere assignment: CCF ML midline at 5700 µm; `ccf_x >= 5700` = left hemisphere.\n- Trial curation for the reference **regression** analyses excludes early-lick / auto-water / free-water / no-response / photostim trials. Our decoder task explicitly requires photostim as an input and early lick, no-lick choice and ignore/miss outcome as outputs, so those trials must be **kept**; we will only exclude auto-water/free-water trials (not real behaviour) if warranted, documented in Step 5.\n\n---\n\n## Step 2: Dataset Exploration\n**Status**: COMPLETE\n\n### Data Structure\n- `/app/data/` contains one directory per mouse: `sub-<subject_id>/` (28 subjects) and `dandiset.yaml` (DANDI:000363, Mesoscale Activity Map dataset, Chen et al.).\n- Each session is one NWB file: `sub-<id>_ses-<YYYYMMDDTHHMMSS>_behavior+ecephys+ogen.nwb`; **174 files total**.\n- All files have identical trial and unit column sets (verified across all 174 files).\n\n**NWB contents (read with `pynwb.NWBHDF5IO`):**\n- `nwb.subject.subject_id` (e.g. `440956`), `nwb.subject.description` = lab mouse name (e.g. `SC015`); `nwb.identifier` = e.g. `SC015_20190207_120657_s1`.\n- `nwb.trials` (`TimeIntervals`), columns: `start_time`, `stop_time`, `trial`, `photostim_onset`, `photostim_power`, `photostim_duration` (strings, `'N/A'` when no stim; onset relative to **trial start**), `trial_uid`, `task` (all `audio delay`), `task_protocol` (all 1), `trial_instruction` (`left`/`right`), `early_lick` (`early`/`no early`), `outcome` (`hit`/`miss`/`ignore`), `auto_water` (0/1), `free_water` (0/1).\n- `nwb.acquisition['BehavioralEvents']` (`BehavioralEvents`), each a `TimeSeries` whose **timestamps** carry the event times (session clock, seconds):\n  `presample_start/stop_times`, `sample_start/stop_times`, `delay_start/stop_times`, `go_start/stop_times` (n == n_trials in **all** 174 sessions), `trialend_start/stop_times`, `left_lick_times`, `right_lick_times`, `photostim_start_times` (data = laser power in mW), `photostim_stop_times`.\n  Note `sample_*` and `delay_*` have **more** events than trials because early licking triggers a **replay** of the sample/delay epoch (confirmed: extra sample events occur only in `early` trials).\n- `nwb.acquisition['BehavioralTimeSeries']`: DeepLabCut side-view (`Camera0_side_`) tracking `JawTracking`, `NoseTracking`, `TongueTracking` (all 174 sessions), occasionally `WhiskerTracking_whisker` (20), `LickPortTracking` (4) and bottom-camera (`Camera3_bottom_*`) series. Each has `data` of shape (n_frames, 3) = (x, y, likelihood) and explicit `timestamps` in session time with **dt = 0.0034 s** (identical in all 174 sessions), segmented per trial: each trial's video segment starts exactly at that trial's `start_time`.\n- `nwb.units`: 39 columns, incl. `spike_times` (session clock), `obs_intervals` (= exactly the (start_time, stop_time) of every trial → **spikes are only recorded within trials**), `unit_quality` (`good`/`multi`, Kilosort-level), **`classification`** (`good`/`unlabelled`, output of the paper's QC classifier), **`anno_name`** (fine CCF annotation string, empty for `unlabelled` units), `is_good_trials` (bool per trial; all True in spot checks), 15 QC metrics (`unit_amp`, `unit_snr`, `isi_violation`, `avg_firing_rate`, `presence_ratio`, `amplitude_cutoff`, `isolation_distance`, `l_ratio`, `d_prime`, `nn_hit_rate`, `nn_miss_rate`, `silhouette_score`, `max_drift`, `cumulative_drift`, `drift_metric`), waveform features, `electrodes` (DynamicTableRegion → CCF `x`,`y`,`z` in µm).\n- `nwb.electrodes`: `location` (JSON with targeted `brain_regions` e.g. `left ALM`), `x`,`y`,`z` CCF coordinates, `shank`, `group_name`.\n- `nwb.electrode_groups`: one per probe insertion; `location` JSON contains coarse target `brain_regions`: left/right ALM, Midbrain, Striatum, Thalamus, Medulla, ECT, BLA.\n\n### Dataset Size (from data files; survey of all 174 files: `/app/cache/survey.py`)\n| Statistic | Value |\n|-----------|-------|\n| Sessions (files) | 174 (173 with ≥1 good unit; 168/174 sessions have stim trials |\n| Unique CCF `anno_name` of good units | 293 |\n\n### Timing facts verified\n- Go cue (`go_start_times`) exists for exactly one per trial in all sessions.\n- `go - trial start`: mean ≈ 3.2 s (min 2.1 s); `trial stop - go`: median ≈ 1.7 s but **min ≈ 0.21 s** — spikes are not observed after `stop_time`, so the tail of the −2.5→+1.5 s window is unobserved in a minority of trials (same in the reference pipeline, which used a −3→+3 s window on the same per-trial data).\n- Last `sample_start` before the go cue is ~1.85–1.95 s before the go cue (tone onset); this matches the paper's sample epoch start at −1.85 s and 1.2 s delay.\n- Tongue `likelihood` is strongly bimodal (≈ 89 % < 0.1, ≈ 10 % > 0.9) → a likelihood threshold cleanly defines tongue visibility.\n\n---\n\n## Step 3: Reference Text Reading\n**Status**: COMPLETE\n\nSources: `/app/methods.txt` (STAR Methods excerpt of the data paper), `/app/datapaper.pdf` (Chen et al. 2024, *Cell* — \"Brain-wide neural activity underlying memory-guided movement\"), `/app/methodpaper.pdf` (Wang*, Kurgyis* et al. 2025, *Nat Neurosci*), `/app/ChenLiuEtAl2023_SpikeSortingQC.pdf`. reference epochs sample [−1.85, −1.2] s, delay [−1.2, 0] s, response [0, 1.5] s.\n- **Binning**: sliding 40 ms window, 3.4 ms stride, rates in Hz (spikes/bin_width). Our task specifies **50 ms bins**, which we implement as non-overlapping 50 ms bins giving rates in Hz (80 bins over −2.5→+1.5 s).\n- **Spike sorting / QC**: Kilosort2 output; 15 quality metrics; five region-specific logistic-regression classifiers (cortex, striatum, thalamus, midbrain, medulla) trained on manual Phy labels; units labelled **`good`** are used for all analyses. In the NWB files this classifier output is the `units.classification` column (`good` vs `unlabelled`), and `anno_name` holds the CCF annotation of classified units. The whitepaper explicitly argues that thresholding individual metrics is inadequate — hence using the provided classifier label is the faithful reproduction of their QC.\n- **Video markers**: DeepLabCut side-view tongue/jaw/nose; outliers detected by 5-sigma velocity threshold and imputed from nearby frames; when the tongue is occluded (in the mouth) the method paper sets tongue position to its mean value. Our decoder task instead requires an explicit \"not visible\" class (class 3), so occlusion is represented as its own category (detected via DLC likelihood).\n- **Region grouping** (reference preprocessing loop): ALM, Medulla, Midbrain, Striatum, Thalamus, Pons, Cerebellum, Hypothalamus, Hippocampus, Orbital, OtherCortex, Olfactory, CorticalSubplate, Pallidum — each split into left/right hemisphere with the CCF ML midline at 5,700 µm.\n\n### Curation Steps\n**Neuron curation rules (reference)**\n1. Keep only units with a CCF/histology annotation (units without histology are dropped).\n2. Keep only units labelled `good` by the QC classifier (25.9 % of Kilosort clusters).\n3. Method-paper analyses additionally drop neurons with mean firing rate < 2 Hz (for firing-rate *prediction* analyses) and brain areas with < 10 neurons per session. These are analysis-specific and are **not** appropriate for the decoding task here (they would discard most of the population available to the decoder), so they are not applied; documented in Step 5.\n\n**Trial curation rules (reference)**\n- \"regular\" trials = no early lick, no auto-water, no free water, no ignore (`correctness != -1`), and no photostimulation.\n- **Our decoder task requires early-lick, photostim, ignore and miss trials** (they are explicit decoder inputs/outputs), so these filters are relaxed; see Step 5.\n- Session inclusion criteria in the data paper (performance > 65 %, ≥ 50 correct left and right trials) are already satisfied by the published sessions.\n\n### Decoders Trained (reference accuracies)\n| Decoded variable | Accuracy |\n|---|---|\n| Choice from behavioral video, pre-sample epoch | AUC 0.51 ± 0.06 (n = 106 sessions) |\n| Choice from behavioral video, sample+delay epochs | AUC 0.66 ± 0.12 |\n| Choice from behavioral video, second half of response epoch | AUC 0.99 ± 0.01 |\n| Choice from single-neuron delay activity (AUC threshold for \"choice-modulated\") | AUC > 0.65 |\n| Uninstructed-movement type from single neurons | AUC > 0.65 threshold |\n\nImplication for our decoder: **choice** should be decodable near-perfectly after the go cue from population activity (video alone gives AUC 0.99); delay-epoch choice information is weaker. Outcome and early-lick should be decodable well above chance; tongue position (a directly observable movement) should be decodable well, since neural activity predicts video markers with high R² in the method paper.\n\n---\n\n## Step 4: Check for Consistency\n**Status**: COMPLETE\n\nI cross-checked the reference code (Step 1), the NWB data (Step 2) and the papers (Step 3). Unlabelled units also lack CCF annotations, so this simultaneously enforces the reference's \"must have histology\" rule. Result: 69,453 units (25.5 % of clusters) vs 69,943 (25.9 %) in the paper.\n2. **No additional firing-rate threshold**: the method paper's ≥ 2 Hz filter and its \"≥10 neurons per area per session\" rule apply to their neuron-wise *encoding* analyses; for population decoding, discarding low-rate neurons throws away usable signal and is not part of the dataset-level curation. Not applied (documented deviation).\n3. **Session curation**: drop sessions with 0 good units → exactly **173** sessions, matching the papers.\n4. **Trial curation**: drop `auto_water == 1` or `free_water == 1` trials (reward delivered independent of the animal's action ⇒ `outcome` is not a behavioural report), matching `get_regular_trial_mask`. **Keep** early-lick, ignore/miss and photostim trials, because the decoder task defines them as outputs/inputs; the reference excluded them only for its encoding analyses.\n5. **Alignment / window / binning**: go-cue aligned, −2.5 → +1.5 s, 80 × 50 ms non-overlapping bins, rates in Hz (counts / 0.05 s). Bin *i* covers [−2.5 + 0.05 i, −2.45 + 0.05 i); the value assigned to input/output time series uses the **bin centre**.\n6. **Unobserved time**: spikes exist only inside `[start_time, stop_time]` (= `obs_intervals`). 96.9 % of trials cover go−2.5 s, 84.4 % cover go+1.5 s (miss trials end early). Bins outside the recorded trial interval necessarily contain 0 spikes; these are kept as 0 (no extra information is available) and the fraction is reported in metadata.\n7. **Tongue visibility threshold**: `likelihood > 0.5`. The likelihood distribution is strongly bimodal (89 % < 0.1, 10 % > 0.9) so the exact threshold is immaterial.\n8. **Percentiles computed per session** over the *binned, visible* tongue-y values of the exported trials, so the resulting class frequencies are exactly 40 / 20 / 40 % of visible bins in each session.\n9. **Outputs are time-varying** (shape (4, 80)): per-trial variables are broadcast across bins, as recommended by the task description.\n10. **Brain regions carry hemisphere** (e.g. `left ALM`), as in the reference (`side_region`), with the CCF ML midline at 5,700 µm.\n\n### Planned Sanity Checks\n- [ ] 173 sessions, 28 subjects, 69,453 neurons after curation.\n- [ ] Per-coarse-region neuron totals reproduce paper values (striatum 7,664; rates = counts / 0.05 s.\n- `tone_onset_times()` — last `sample_start_times` at/ before the go cue per trial (handles early-lick epoch replays).\n- `photostim_binary()` — binary per-bin photostim indicator from `photostim_start/stop_times` events (bin counted as on if it overlaps the laser interval).\n- `bin_tongue()` — DLC side-camera tongue y averaged per 50 ms bin over frames with `likelihood > 0.5`, after 5σ velocity outlier rejection (method paper); NaN when no valid frame.\n- `discretize_tongue()` — per-session 40th/60th percentiles of the binned visible y → classes 0/1/2, NaN → 3.\n- `convert_session()` — loads one NWB with `pynwb`, curates units/trials, builds neural/input/output arrays and a `session_info` record with timings and QC statistics.\n- `make_processing_plots()` — 8-panel diagnostics per session (`--show-processing`): raw spike raster vs binned rates for one trial, population PSTH computed independently from raw spike times vs the converted neural mean, inputs vs raw event times, raw tongue trace vs binned values and percentile thresholds, resulting discrete tongue classes, per-trial outputs, tongue-class time course.\n- `main()` — parallel over sessions (`ProcessPoolExecutor`, default 16 workers), assembles the target dictionary, writes the pickle, prints summary statistics.\n\nEfficiency:\n- Spike times are read once per unit; binning is vectorised with `searchsorted` over concatenated bin edges (0.16 s/session for ~450 neurons × 400 trials).\n- Unit → electrode lookup uses the `VectorIndex` arrays directly instead of per-unit `units['electrodes'][i]` DataFrame construction (~100× faster; verified to give identical electrode ids).\n- Video tracking arrays are read once per session and binned with `np.bincount`.\n- Sessions are processed in parallel (16 workers), so the wall-clock cost is dominated by pickling the ~10 GB result.\n\nIssue found and fixed during development: **trials with no ephys at all**. In 100 sessions some trials (4.35 % overall; 2 sessions where the probes stop long before the behaviour: 376/582 and 321/480 trials) contain zero spikes from *every* good unit over the whole trial. NWB does not flag them (`is_good_trials` is all-True and `obs_intervals` simply mirror the trials table). Such trials are excluded as invalid data periods.\n\n---\n\n## Step 7: Sample Conversion and Validation\n**Status**: COMPLETE\n\n`python -u /app/convert_data.py /app/sample_data.pkl --sample --show-processing` → `/app/conversion_sample_out.txt`;\n`python -u /app/train_decoder.py /app/sample_data.pkl --verify-only` → `/app/verification_sample_out.txt` (**no errors, no warnings**).\n\n### Sample Statistics (2 sessions of mouse 440956 / SC015)\n| Statistic | Value |\n|-----------|-------|\n| Sessions | 2 |\n| Neurons (total) | 834 |\n| Neurons / session | 459, 375 |\n| Subjects | 1 |\n| Trials (total) | 513 (of 834 raw;     'metadata': {\n            'dataset': 'Mesoscale Activity Map (DANDI:000363), Chen et al. 2024 Cell; '\n# Decisions\n\n## 1-a. How are **all the data** for all subjects, sessions, and trials loaded in?\n\ni. The dataset is distributed as one NWB file per session under `data/sub-<subject_id>/`. All sessions are found with a single glob over that layout, and each file is opened with `pynwb` and processed once. Subjects, trials, and units are then read from within each file (`nwb.subject`, `nwb.trials`, `nwb.units`, `nwb.acquisition`).\n\nii. Finding all data:\n```python\nfiles = sorted(glob.glob(os.path.join(DATA_DIR, 'sub-*', '*.nwb')))\n...\nfor i, path in enumerate(files, 1):\n    res = process_session(path)\n```\n\nLoading one session:\n```python\nwith NWBHDF5IO(path, mode='r', load_namespaces=True) as io:\n    nwb = io.read()\n    units = nwb.units\n    trials = nwb.trials.to_dataframe()\n    bev = nwb.acquisition['BehavioralEvents'].time_series\n```\n\niii. NWB is the published format for this dataset and `pynwb` is its standard reader. Since there is one file per session, the directory listing is the complete set of sessions and a glob is sufficient; sorting it makes the session order deterministic. The resulting counts (174 files, 28 subjects) match `assetsSummary` in `data/dandiset.yaml`.\n\n## 1-b. How are the data split into subjects?\n\ni. Each NWB file records its animal in `nwb.subject.subject_id`, a numeric string such as `'440956'`. That value is read for every session and carried through to assembly, where `subjects` is the sorted set of unique ids and `subject_idx` gives each session's index into that list.\n\nii. Per session:\n```python\nreturn {\n    'session_id': nwb.identifier,\n    'subject': nwb.subject.subject_id,\n    ...\n```\n\nAt assembly:\n```python\nsubjects = sorted({r['subject'] for r in results})\nsub_ix = {s: i for i, s in enumerate(subjects)}\n...\n'subjects': subjects,\n'subject_idx': np.array([sub_ix[r['subject']] for r in results], np.int32),\n```\n\niii. `subject_id` is the canonical animal identifier in the file, and the containing folder name (`sub-440956`) is derived from it, so no separate grouping step is needed. This gives 28 subjects with 3-10 sessions each, matching the dandiset. The numeric id differs from the mouse name used in the papers — `nwb.identifier` is e.g. `SC015_20190207_120657_s1`, so subject `440956` is mouse `SC015` — but the numeric id is what the NWB subject field provides, so it is used directly.\n\n## 1-c. How are the data split into sessions?\n\ni. One NWB file is one session, so no grouping or splitting is needed. Each session is identified by `nwb.identifier` (e.g. `SC015_20190207_120657_s1`, encoding mouse, date, time and session number), recorded per session and also listed in `metadata['session_info']`. Session order in the output follows the sorted file list.\n\nii.\n```python\nfiles = sorted(glob.glob(os.path.join(DATA_DIR, 'sub-*', '*.nwb')))\n```\n\n```python\n'session_id': nwb.identifier,\n```\n\n```python\n'session_info': [\n    {'session_id': r['session_id'], 'subject': r['subject'],\n     'n_trials': r['n_trials'], 'n_units': r['n_units']}\n    for r in results\n],\n```\n\niii. The dandiset already stores one session per file, so the file boundary is the session boundary and nothing has to be inferred. Because the filename embeds the acquisition timestamp (`sub-440956_ses-20190207T120657_...`), sorting the paths puts sessions in chronological order within each subject. 173 of the 174 files reach the output; the one exception is dropped for having no quality-controlled units (see 2-c).\n\n## 1-d. Are the data correctly split into trials?\n\ni. Trials come from the NWB trials table (`nwb.trials`), one row per behavioural trial, with exactly one go-cue event per row. The row count is checked against the number of go-cue events.\n\nii.\n```python\ntrials = nwb.trials.to_dataframe()\ngo = np.asarray(bev['go_start_times'].timestamps)\nassert len(go) == len(trials), f'{len(go)} go cues vs {len(trials)} trials'\n```\n\niii. Trials are clearly defined by the trials table, so it is used directly rather than re-deriving boundaries from the event streams. `go_start_times` has exactly one event per trial in all 174 sessions, which makes the mapping unambiguous. This is not true of the other trial-phase events: `sample_start_times` and `delay_start_times` can have several entries per trial, because a lick during the sample or delay replays that epoch.\n\n## 1-e. How are trials filtered based on quality controls?\n\ni. Trials are filtered only for absence of spike data, in two cases. First, trials outside `units/obs_intervals`: in 8 sessions the ephys recording starts after the behaviour, leaving up to 376 leading trials with no spikes. Second, `free_water` trials, which have no spikes anywhere in the window even though `obs_intervals` covers them. A session is dropped entirely if fewer than 2 trials survive. No behavioural quality filter is applied.\n\nii.\n```python\n# filter behavioral trials with no spike data\noi_off = np.asarray(units['obs_intervals'].data)\noi_start = np.concatenate([[0], oi_off[:-1]])\nobs = np.asarray(units['obs_intervals'].target.data)[oi_start[good[0]]:oi_off[good[0]]]\nkeep = np.isin(np.round(trials['start_time'].values, 4), np.round(obs[:, 0], 4))\nassert keep.sum() == len(obs), f'{keep.sum()} matched vs {len(obs)} observed'\n\n# filter no water trials\nkeep &= trials['free_water'].values == 0\nif keep.sum() < 2:\n    return None\ntrials = trials[keep]\ngo = go[keep]\n```\n\niii. `obs_intervals` is the file's own record of which trials were observed, and its start times match `trials.start_time`, which makes the mapping exact. The `free_water` exclusion was found empirically — those trials are covered by `obs_intervals` yet contain no spikes at all — and accounts for 2,449 of the 2,451 all-zero trials remaining after the `obs_intervals` filter.\n\nEarly-lick and no-response (`ignore`) trials are deliberately kept, even though the data paper states \"Early lick trials and no response trials were excluded for analysis\", because both are required decoder outputs here. The 2-trial minimum is the target format's requirement.\n\nTogether these remove 3,510 of the 94,370 trials in the retained sessions (3.7%), leaving 90,860.\n\n## 2-a. What variables in the raw data is the final `neural` data derived from?\n\ni. Neural data is derived from `units/spike_times`, the sorted spike times of each unit in session-absolute seconds. Only units with `classification == 'good'` contribute (see 2-c). The go-cue times (`BehavioralEvents/go_start_times`) are the other input, used to place the bin edges.\n\nii.\n```python\noffs = np.asarray(units['spike_times'].data)\nallst = np.asarray(units['spike_times'].target.data)\nstarts = np.concatenate([[0], offs[:-1]])\n\nedges = (go[:, None] + REL_EDGES[None, :]).ravel()\nrates = np.empty((good.size, n_trials, N_BINS), np.float32)\nfor r, u in enumerate(good):\n    s = allst[starts[u]:offs[u]]\n```\n\niii. `spike_times` is the only neural representation in the file, so firing rates are computed from it directly.\n\n## 2-b. How is the `neural` data processed?\n\ni. Spike times are converted to per-bin firing rates in Hz. For each good unit, the bin edges for every trial are built as one flat array of absolute times, `np.searchsorted` gives the running spike count at each edge, and differencing adjacent counts gives the spike count per bin. Counts are divided by the bin width to give Hz. No smoothing, normalisation, or baseline subtraction is applied.\n\nii.\n```python\nedges = (go[:, None] + REL_EDGES[None, :]).ravel()\nrates = np.empty((good.size, n_trials, N_BINS), np.float32)\nfor r, u in enumerate(good):\n    s = allst[starts[u]:offs[u]]\n    # running spike total at each edge; differencing gives the count per bin\n    pos = np.searchsorted(s, edges).reshape(n_trials, N_BINS + 1)\n    rates[r] = np.diff(pos, axis=1)\nrates /= BIN                                  # counts -> Hz\n```\n\niii. Firing rate is computed from the binned spike count over the 50 ms window defined in the instructions. This also matches the reference code, which calls `sliding_histogram(..., rate=True)` and returns `binSpikes / bin_width`.\n\n## 2-c. How is the `neural` data filtered based on quality controls?\n\ni. Only units with `units/classification == 'good'` are kept. No thresholds are applied to any individual quality metric. A session with no such units is dropped entirely. This retains 69,453 of 272,227 units (25.5%), a median of 390 per session.\n\nii.\n```python\n# ---- units: QC classifier verdict ----------------------------------\ncls = _text(units['classification'])\ngood = np.flatnonzero(cls == 'good')\nif good.size == 0:\n    return None\n```\n\niii. `classification` is the verdict of the spike-sorting quality-control classifier described in `ChenLiuEtAl2023_SpikeSortingQC.pdf`.\n\n`units/unit_quality` ('good' / 'multi') is deliberately not used: it is an older label that disagrees on 12.2% of the classifier-good units and is far more permissive.\n\nThe one dropped session (`sub-440958_ses-20190216T162508`) has `classification` and `anno_name` set to NaN for all 1,852 units, i.e. it was never quality-controlled. Excluding it gives 173 sessions and 69,453 good units, against the white paper's 173 sessions and 69,943 units.\n\n## 2-d. How is the per-trial `neural` data aligned to the event described in the `instructions`?\n\ni. Spike times and event times are already on the same session-absolute clock, so no alignment step is needed. The bin edges relative to the go cue are added to each trial's go-cue time to give the absolute time window for that trial, and the spikes are binned against those edges directly.\n\nii.\n```python\ngo = np.asarray(bev['go_start_times'].timestamps)\n```\n\n```python\nedges = (go[:, None] + REL_EDGES[None, :]).ravel()\nrates = np.empty((good.size, n_trials, N_BINS), np.float32)\nfor r, u in enumerate(good):\n    s = allst[starts[u]:offs[u]]\n    pos = np.searchsorted(s, edges).reshape(n_trials, N_BINS + 1)\n    rates[r] = np.diff(pos, axis=1)\n```\n\niii. Everything in the NWB file is timestamped on one global clock, so aligning to the go cue only requires looking up each trial's go-cue time and taking the window around it. There is no resampling or interpolation, and no per-stream offset to correct.\n\n## 2-e. How is the `neural` data temporally binned/resampled?\n\ni. Spike times are binned into 80 non-overlapping 50 ms bins spanning -2.5 s to +1.5 s relative to the go cue. The bin grid is defined once, as 81 edges relative to the go cue, and reused for every trial and session, so every trial has the same 80 timepoints.\n\nii.\n```python\n# trial window relative to the go cue, and bin width, in seconds\nT_START, T_STOP = -2.5, 1.5\nBIN = 0.05\nN_BINS = int(round((T_STOP - T_START) / BIN))             \n\nREL_EDGES = T_START + BIN * np.arange(N_BINS + 1)         \nCENTERS = REL_EDGES[:-1] + BIN / 2                        \n```\n\n```python\nedges = (go[:, None] + REL_EDGES[None, :]).ravel()\n```\n\niii. The window and the 50 ms bin width are set by the instructions. Defining the grid once as offsets from the go cue gives a constant 80 timepoints per trial, which the target format requires.\n\n## 3-a. What variables in the raw data is `input` *time_from_tone_onset* derived from?\n\ni. From `sample_start_times`, the tone onsets of the session, together with the go cue of each trial. The tone taken for a trial is the **last one** before its go cue.\n\nii. The tone of each trial:\n```python\nsample = np.asarray(bev['sample_start_times'].timestamps)\ntone = sample[np.searchsorted(sample, go, side='left') - 1]\n```\n\niii. An early lick replays the sample epoch, so a trial can carry more than one tone; the last one before the go cue is the one the animal actually used.\n\n## 3-b. No additional processing needed other than find the tone onset time.\n\n## 3-c. How is `input` *time_from_tone_onset* aligned with the neural data?\n\ni. N/A\n\n## 4-a. What variables in the raw data is `input` *photostim* derived from?\n\ni. Frames with `likelihood < 0.5` are set to NaN, since the tracker still reports a position when the tongue is not protruding. The surviving values are averaged into 50 ms bins across the whole session, and the 40th and 60th percentiles of *those bin means* give two class edges. Each trial's window is then binned the same way and digitised against those edges, giving classes 0/1/2. Bins containing no visible frame are assigned a fourth class, `3` (`'not visible'`).\n\nii.\n```python\nTONGUE_CONF = 0.5                # tracking likelihood for the tongue to count as visible\nTONGUE_PCT = (40, 60)            # per-session percentiles -> 3 visible classes\nTONGUE_HIDDEN = 3                # no visible tongue frame in the bin\n```\n\n```python\ny[data[:, 2] < TONGUE_CONF] = np.nan     # keep only visible frames\n\n# bin the whole session on one grid, then take percentiles of the bin means\ngidx = np.floor((t_cam - t_cam[0]) / BIN).astype(np.int64)\nedges = np.nanpercentile(_bin_mean(gidx, y, int(gidx[-1]) + 1), TONGUE_PCT)\n\n# per trial, bin the same way and digitise against those edges\ncls = np.full((len(go), N_BINS), TONGUE_HIDDEN, np.int8)\nlo = np.searchsorted(t_cam, go + T_START, 'left')\nhi = np.searchsorted(t_cam, go + T_STOP, 'left')\nfor i in range(len(go)):\n    b = np.floor((t_cam[lo[i]:hi[i]] - (go[i] + T_START)) / BIN).astype(np.int64)\n    np.clip(b, 0, N_BINS - 1, out=b)\n    m = _bin_mean(b, y[lo[i]:hi[i]], N_BINS)\n    ok = ~np.isnan(m)\n    cls[i, ok] = np.digitize(m[ok], edges)\n```\n\niii. The tongue is visible in only ~10% of frames, and when it is retracted the tracker still emits a position, so those frames are discarded rather than averaged in — including them shifts the percentiles and mixes real protrusions with noise. The 40th/60th split and the per-session scope both follow the instructions. A fourth class is defined for bins with no visible tongue, which is 75% of all bins.\n\n## 8-d. How is `output` *tongue_y_position* aligned with the neural data?\n\ni. This is the one genuinely time-varying output, so it is the only one needing real alignment. On the ~3% of trials where the go cue falls less than 2.5 s after trial start, the leading bins therefore contain no frames at all and fall into the `'not visible'` class.\n\n## 9. Where nothing was recorded, the session or trial is excluded, since emitting it would fabricate data — a trial with no spikes would otherwise appear as 4 s of 0 Hz across every unit.
